Here, to begin itb, you will see, are some -pretty enuarerrs costumes tor iancv dress Daus. The first is "The Queen of Hearts:" Of this the hem, band, short skirt, and puff sleeves arc in white satin Merveilieux. There is a low. Prittass•-

tunic, draped high on the hips, in purple Sarah silk and trimmed with one large and several small hearts in ermine. Girdle and tasselled satchel in crimson velvet studded with gold and silver hearts. White gauze fan displaying silver, gold, and red hearts, mother o' pearl mount. Red crystal hearts in the coiffure and On the white kid shoes. Gilt crown. Another costume is a Louis XV. Riding Habit. The skirt is raised on the left hip in fawn- coloured cloth, braided in brown and gold. Close- fitting bodice, with large elbow sleeves in either hunter's-green cloth or Bengaline silk, relieved with • basgue, pla.stron, flat collar, and pointed cuffs in red velvet, wrought with gold. Flat gilt buttons, white silk sash, fringed with gold. Puflings in ivory muslin. Fawn felt hat ornamented with varie- gated plumes. . . _

Flow- ers lend themselves ;n an effective way for fancy dresses. Such a one is a " da.ffoclil" with olive green bodi...T, pale orange skirt, and len-on yellow petals. Other !lowers, roses iii partieulat,

_a suitable for fancy dresses, the various shades of the blossoms allowing the intending wearer to select the most suitable to her complexion. For children the style 13 as charming as for young girls. I remember some of last year's costumes at the Lord Mayor's fancy dress ball were lovely things; and yet they were not hard to make. For instance, some Welsh children came in Stuart costume, the little boys wearing knee breeches and coats of grey plush, with lace miles, and the little girls long frocks'ef white satin and pearls, with close coifs of rare old lace upon their fair hair. I was very pleased with a trio of "Paddies from Cork," in Irish frieze, with blackthorns and red handker• chiefs, and there were several naval and military uniforms correctly reproduced in miniature among the boys, as well as such variants as tropical full dress in duck with coloured cummerbund, and in such obselete patterns as might have been worn at aterloo. One of these latter was well suited for a partner in a very smart little rivandien3 in red, white, and blue. For many of the girls very happy inspirations had been drawn from the Empire, Ineroyahle, Merveillense, and " 1830" sources, which seem to he growing in popularity on these occasions—doubtless because they permit of the colour combinations most becoming to their wearers.

One of the prettiest costumes, however, was an "Empire lady "—a girl of about 13. She was wearing a Greek frock in heliotrope satin Duchesse, lined with a deeper tone, and elaborately trimmed with silver and pearl embroidery. Crossbands of satin, enriched with precious stones or jet caboc.hons, sparklcp3 ott the balloon sleeves, and -draped under a jewel ornament the low opening of

should be worn, and the youthful noble- man might carry a little trumpet slung round the shoulder. Another jolly little costume is the Eight of Diamonds. (Of course, any other card would do almost as well). It is for a little girl and a huge card is worn on the front and back of the * little smock, ala sandwich man. Toe white back- ground should be of silk, and the " pips " in red stuff of some sort. Then there is a little Chinese lady with a huge fan, and little Mother Hubbard, with a dress and muff covered with white fur; but I have not space to descriLe them all. There are some pretty examples of ladies' redin- gotes or pelisses this season; they are extremely smart both for walking or visiting. Fancy woollen materials or cloth in a plain shade of colour are used to make these pelisses. A charming model has a square cut yoke of velvet, the straight skirt which is attached to the yoke is of cloth the same shade, as are also the bishop sleeves; the base of the yoke is outlined with a border of grey fur, which is carried round the sleeves to simullste epaulettes, more of the same fur is used to edge the collar and cuffs. All the new capes are cut to fit flat over the shoulders; they are composed of black and coloured cloths and velvets. Bands of fur are the chief trimmings, which are used to outline the borders of these capes. Dresses, too, have fur trimmings, which add much ,to their effect. One of the most stylish I have seen was of purple Venetian cloth, trimmed with either sable or fox fur. The square front was of ivory cloth but it could be braided with satin. 1,1 4

skirts are ....I plain although bodices remain somewhat fanciful. For evening, wear there are as usual sonic exceedingly charming toilettes. One of these is a combination of eau-de-nil silk, white lace, pearls and pearl ornaments The _plain skirt is lined throughout, the lower part being interlined with haircloth ; the front is &le with darts at the waist, while the fulness at the back is pleated and secured to the band, which is covered with silk. The tight-fitting bodice is cut with a slightly pointed basque front and back, where it laces in the centre. The neck is cut round at the back and square in front, and trimmed across the shoulders and round the back with two rows of pearls, thee rows of the same being arranged across the front, and decorated with three handsome drop ornaments of the same. The shoulders are also decorated with small pearl orna- ments. The edge of bodice is neatened with a fold of ribbon fastened at the back under a butterfly bow of the same. The full puff sleeves are lined with muslin, and gathered over a plain foundation, then gathered into the armhole with an eciaulette of lace.

About. hats one has not much to say at present, and those I have desgribed to. you within the last few weeks comprise all the most tasteful designs. However, here is one which I am pretty sure you will like, unless your tastes are less simple than I thought. It is a very simple hat and is well worth notice. The chapeau is made of blue felt, with a large ruche of blue and green .shot silk gathered round the crown.

Children's cloaks area matter of taste, and may be made of thick .Uath-coating, camel's-hair, or lambs- wool for winter, and silk, serge, or merino for sum- mer. A most stylish one is neatly circular, with two capes, round behind, and• pointed in front. It is well to make it longer than the frocks, so as to well cover the feet, and to supersede the fur trim- niing in summer by frilled lace. There should be a flap down the front under the fur, in which the buttouholes are set to fasten it. This cloak may be made in two halves, or cut in one, according to the single or double width of the stuff. When the child can walk, it should have pelisses which are mimic very much on the plan of the petticoat yoke, bodice, and skirt, but with sleeves of a coat shape down to the wrists, and a cape of the game material prettily trimmed. It will take about two yards of yard-wide material, and whether fastened by ribbons or buttons, lir these fastenings be quickly amomplished as his lordship's and lady- ship's patienoe is limited.

...:ren's out-door winter costumes are as pretty as they always are. I should like you to notice particularly, a little bonnet for children known as the Normandy. It is a most aflinirable model, its shape boasting a large velvet crown and curved brim turned back with a light-toned silk, and boasting no trimming save a gathered resette. It lends itself to any material, and can of course be made in any colour to match a coat. Your loving

London domestic servants number in all 206,000. They are in the service of 476,425 persons, representing 113 per cent, of the families of the Metropolis. Technically, any inhabitant of the United Kingdom is liable to be called upon to undertake the uncongenial task of hangman. The salary is a week as a retain- ing fee, and £2 after an execution. - . Notwithstandlng the enthusiasm with which cycling is now pursued by ladies, there are plenty who believe it to be a passing, craze. A Society man, who makes it his business, to know all about Society doings, his offered to lay heavy odds that the craze will be out of date in three years' time.

Seek the eunlight is the advice of all present-day hygienists. Patients on the sunny side of the hospital ward recover soonest. The person who always walks on the sunny side of the street outlives his shade-seeking brother by ten years. Sleep in rooms where the sun has shed his rays all day. Bask in the sun all you can.
Piano Playing Produces' "Nerves."

A corresponding member of the Paris Academy ot Medicine has sent to that learned body a memoir in which he maintains that the numerous cases of chloro- sis, neurosis, and neurasthenia observed among young girls is due to learning to play on the piano and the hours devoted to practising. He has drawn up careful statistics from which he concludes that, among six thou- sand pupils obliwed, before attaining the age of twelve, to play the piano, nearly twelve per cent, suffer from nervoui troubles. The author does not attempt to draw up statistics of the victims among persons who have to listen to their performances.

s- . . The Care of Lamps. There are a gteat-triany people wno bay wad lamps all tbeir lives, who know absolutely nothing about their proper care. They wash chimneys with soap and water and cut the wicks down beyond the charred part, and lean back with satisfaction, believing their work has been well and properly done. In point of fact, the chimney of a lamp should never be touched with water. A few clrrps of alcohol will remove the dim.smoky effect and make the chimney as brisht RS possible when it is polished with soft flannel or chamois skin. There ilI then be no danger of any moisture bang left in the chimney so that it will crack when the lamp is lighted. All parts of the burner of a lamp should be thoroughly clean. A little kerose.ne or alcohol on a cloth is as good for this purpose as anything else to clean the burner, providing it is polished clean and dry afterwards. Neg- lected old burners may be boiled in soda and water and renew their usefulness, though not their appearance, as this process removes the lacquer put on most brass. It is not necessary to allow a burner to get in such a con- dition that it must be boiled in this way to clean it, but if it does there is no better remedy. 'Every part of the outside of a lamp should be rubbed dry and free from oil when it is filled daily. Do not cut the wick of a lamp after it is first put in and has berm evenly trimmed once, but each day brush off the charred portion. The wick will last longer, and the light be evener and clearer if this last rule is strictly adhered to. Metal or porcelain lamps in which the oil is put in a font of metal resting within the porcelain are the most desirable and least dangerous lamps to use. .•

Rejoicing in her freedom, Ctp galloped down to the water's edge, and then walked her horse up and down along the course of t stream until she found a good fording phica_t. Then gathering up bet riding-skirt and throwing it over the neck of her horse, she plunged boldly into the stream, and with the water splashing and foaming all around her, urged him onward until they crossed the river and climbed up the opposite bank. A bridle-path lay before her, leading from the fording place through a deep wood. That path attracted her; she followed it, charmed alike by the solitude of the wood, the novelty of the scene, and her own sense of freedom. But one thought was given to the story of Black Donald, and that was a re-assur- ing one. "If Black Donald is a mail-robber, then this little bridle-path is far enough off his beat." And so saying, she gaily galloped along, singing as she went, following the narrow path up hill and down dale through the wintry woods. Drawn on by the attraction of the unknown, and deceiving herself by the continued repetition of one resolve, namely: " When I get to the top of the next bill, and see what lies beyond, then I will turn back," she galloped on and on—on and on—on and on! until she had put several miles between herself and her home, until her horse began to exhibit signs of weariness, and the level rays of the setting sun were striking redly through the leafless branches of the trees.

Cap drew rein on the top of a high, wooded hill, and looked about her. On her left hand the sun was sinking like a ball of fire below the horizon; all around her everywhere were the wintry woods; far away, in the direction whence she had come, she saw the tops of the meuntains behind Hurricane Hall, looking like blue clouds against the southern horizon; the Hall itself and the river below were out of sight. "I wonder bow far I am from home ?" said Capitola, uneasily; "somewhere between six and seven miles, I reckon. Dear me, I didn't mean to ride so far. I've got over a great deal of ground In these two hours. I shall not get back so soon; my horse is tired to death ; it will take me three hours to reach Hurricane Hall. Good gracious, it will be pitch dark before I get there. No, thank heaven' there'll be a moon. But won't there be a row, though! Whew I Well, I must turn about and lose no time. Come, Gyp! get up, Gyp I good horse we're going home!" And so saying, Capitola, turned her horse's head and urged him into a gallop. She bad gone on for about a mile, and it was growing dark, and her horse was again slackening his pace, when she thought she heard the sound of another horse's hoofs behind her. She drew rein and listened, and was sure of it. Now, without being the least of a coward, Capitols thought of the loneliness of the woods, and the lateness of the hour, her own helple-sness, and—Black Donald I And thinking " uiscretion tho better part of valour," she urged her horse once more into a gallop, for a few hundred yards; bat the jaded beast soon broke into a trot, and subsided into a walk that threatened won to come to a stand- till.
_ The invisible pursuer gained on her. In vain she urged her steed with whip and voice ; the poor beast would obey and trot for a few yards, and then fall into a walk.
The thundering footfalls of the pursuing horse were close in the rear.
"Oh, Gyp is it possible that, instead of my capturing Black Donald, you are going to let Black Dmald or somebcdy el,e catch me 7" exclaimed Capitola, in mock despair, as she urged her wearied steed.
In vain The pursuing horseman was beside her! a strong hand was laid upon her bridle I a mocking voice was whispering in her ear: " Whith.er away so last, pretty one 1"
CHATTER. XVI.
CAP'S PEARFUL ADVENTURE. 44 Who passes by this road so late? Companion of the Majolaine ! Who passes by this road so late? Say 1 oh, say 1" —OLD FRENCH SONO.
Of a naturally strong constitution and adventur- ous disposition, and inured from infancy to danger, Capitola possessed a high degree of courage, self- control, and plesence of mind.

At the touch of that ruthless hand, at the sound of that gibing voice, all her faculties instantly collected and concentrated themselves upon the emergency. As by a flash of lightning she saw every feature of her imminent danger—the loneli- ness of the woods, the lateness of the hoar, the recklessness of her fes.rful companion, and her own
weakness. In another instant her resolution was taken and her course determined. So, when the stranger repeated his mocking question: "Whither away so fast, pretty one 1" she answered with animation:

"Oh, I am going home, and so glad to have com- pany; for indeed I was dreadfully afraid of riding alone through these woods to-night l" "Afraid, pretty one—what of 7" "Oh, of ghosts and witches, wild beasts, runaway negroes and—Black Donald l"_

"Then you are tot afraid of me "Lore( no, indeed I I guess I ain't! why should I be afraid of a. Tespectable-looking gentleman like you, sir 7" "And so you are going borne—where is your home, pretty one Y' "On the other side of the river; but you need not keep on calling me 'pretty one,' it must be as tiresome to you to repeat it as it is to me to hear it."

"What shall 1 call you, then, my dear ?" "You may call me Miss Black, or if you are friendly, you may call me Ctipitola." "CAPITOLA I" exclaimed the man, in a deep and charuzed voice, as he dropped her bridle. "Yes, Capitola what objection have you got to that? It is a pretty name, isn't it ? but if you feel wry friendly, you may call me Cap," "Well, then, my pretty Cap, where do you live across the river ?" asked the stranger, recovering his self-possession. "Oh, at a rum old place they call Hurricane Hall, with a rum old military officer they call Old Hurricane," said Capitola, for the first time stealing a sidelong glance at her fearful companion.

It was not Black Donald—that was the first conclusion to which she rashly jumped. He ap- peared to be a gentlemanly ruffian about forty years of age, well dressed in a black riding suit; black beaver hat drawn down close over his eyes; black hair and whiskers; heavy black eyebrows that met across his nose; drooping eyelashes, and eyes that looked out under the corners of the lids; alto- gether a sly, sinister, cruel face a cross between fox and tiger I it warned Capitola to expect no mercy there! After the girl's last words he seemed to have fallen into thought for a moment, and then again he spoke: "Well, my pretty Cap, how long have you been living at Hurricane Hall ?" "Ever since my guardian, Major Warfield, brought me from the city of New York, where I received my education—(in the streets)," she ment- ally added. "Hump why did you ride so fast, my pretty Cap ?" he asked, eyeing her from the corner of his eyes. "Oh, sir, because I was afraid, as I told you be- fore; afraid of runaway negroes and wild beasts, and so on—but now with a good gentleman like you I don't feel afraid at all; and I'm very glad to be able to walk poor Gyp; because he's tired, poor fellow'!" " Yes, poor fellow " said the traveller, in a mock- ing tone, "he is tired; suppose you dismount and let him rest. Come, I'll get off, too, and we will sit down here by the roadside and have a friendly con- versation." _

Capitols stole a glance at his face. Yes, notwith- standing his light tone, be was grimly in earnest: there was no mercy to be expected from that sly, sinister, cruel face. "Come, my pretty Cap, what say you 7" "I don't care if I do," she said, riding to the edge of the path, drawing rein, and looking down as if to examine the ground. "Come, little beauty, must I help you off?" asked the stranger. " N-n-uo," answered Capitola, with deliberate hesitation, "no, this is not a good place to sit down and talk; it's all full of brambles." "Very well; shall we go on a little farther ?" "Oh. yes; but I don't want to ride fast, because It will tire my horse." "You shall go just as you please, my angel," said the traveller. "I wonder whether this wretch thinks me very simple or very depraved—he must have come to one or the other conclusion," thought Capitola. They rode on very slowly for a mile further, and then having arrived at an open glade, the stranger drew rein, and said "Come, pretty lark, hop down! here's a nice place to sit and rest." • -”--YerY wont come help me off V! Bail Capitols.

div.head: Small Butchers' Bills.
div.p: Small Butchers' Bills.

The subjoined hints from " Cassell's Household Guide" will perhaps be useful :—The most profitable joint which can possibly t,e bought for tbe use of a household is the top side of the round of beef. It is not a cheap joinr, but it can be used all through, and not a particle need be wasted. If the meat is of good quality, is carefully conked, and well hasted. it is tender and juicy. If care- lessly cooked it will be dry and hard. Thick• flank of beef and the leg of mutton piece of beef are also prefi,:- able. The thin end of the flank and the brisket and the aitchbore of beef cost less per pound, but they Are dear because there is so much waste with them, especially for children, who will not eat fat and gristle. A sirloin of beef is an excellent joint, but it is generally and rightly considered an expensive one. Yet it may be used so as to turn it to very good account. Unless there is a family weakness for fat, it should never be cooked with the fl on. Rather the flap should be cut straight off, then salted and boiled, pressed and glazed, when it is rxcel- lent. Or a little ox kidney and a few tinned oysters should be put with it, and it should be made into a pie, when it will be delicious. The housekeeper, when pur- chasing a sirloin of beef, will do well to think of this way of using the flap, and buy a joint weighing a pound or two :nore for the purpose of trying it. :die may thus obtain a better cut, and will certainly reap an advan- tage. Sometimes the under cut of a sirloin is taken out and conked. -sepavateli like mums,. steak. Colains,A_ sir- loin is, however, so excellent that it is questionable hether the plan is a good one. When a sirloin of beef is no longer fit to be brought to table, there is always a great deal of meat on it which can be used for rissoles, croquettes, sausage rolls, Cornish pasties, shepherd's pie, bcc., Stl.. and there is fat which can be rendered down for dripping. Hard sinewy parts of meat genet, ally cost little, and are very good if stewed long and gently. Of this nature are the roll of the blade-bone of beef, the muscle of the leg of beef, and the sera!, end of a neck of mutton. Meat of this kind should be stewed Ir na and gently for a long time—five or six hours. It will then be found excellent, and will supply cheap and good dinners at a trifling cost.

div.head: CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BY MRS. E. D. E. N. So I.7TriNVORTH.
div.p: CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BY MRS. E. D. E. N. So I.7TriNVORTH.
CHAPTER XV. CAP'S COUNTRY CAPERS. "A wilful elf—an uncle's child, That half a pet and half a pest, Was still reproved, endured, caressed Yet never tamed, though never spoiled."

Capitola at first was delighted and half incredu- lous at the great change in her fortunes. The spacious and comfortable mansion of which she found herself the little mistress; the high rank of the veteran officer who claimed her as his ward and niece; the abundance, regularity, and respect ability of her new life; the leisure, the privacy, the attendance of servants, were all so entirely different from anything to which she had previously been accustomed, that there were times when she doubted its reality, and distrusted her own identity or her sanity. Sometimes, of a morning, after a very vivid dream of the alleys, cellars, and gutters, rags- pickers, newsboys, and beggars of New York, she would open her eyes upon her own comfort- able chamber, with its glowing fire and crimson curtains, its bright mirror crowning the walnut bureau between them, and would jump up and gaze wildly around, not remembering where she was, or how she came thither.

Sometimes, suddenly started by an intense realisation of the contrast between her past and her present life, she would mentally inquire: "Can this be really I myself, and not another? I, the little houseless wanderer through the streets and alleys of New York 1,. the little news-girl in boy's clothes? I, the wretched little vagrant that was brought up before the Recorder, and was about to be sent to V-- Tr 7' fuge for juvenile delinquent-, ? C. apitola, the little outcast of the c . into Miss Black, the young lady, ress of a fine old country scat! c I military officer un7l,-, •

come of po-olsab- money settled t ag carriages, and I horses, and serva-il lel No ;it can't be! its just iv —I see how it is. I'm crazy, that', -.hat L.iazy I For now I think of it, the 1; I giber of my former life was being -.4iglairl . the Recorder for wearing boy's elf !)•:.P. Nee. : a sure that it was upon that occasi t I went suddenly mad with trouble, and all • is a IL 1 atic's fancy. This fine old countr'ch I vainly think myself the mistress, is just the pauper mad-house to which the magistrates have sent me. This fine old military officer whom I call my uncle is the bead-doctor. The servants who come at my call are the keepers. There is DO figure out of my past life in my present one, except Herbert Greyson. But, pshaw I be is not ' the nephew of his uncle!' he is only my old comrade Herbert Greyson, the sailor lad, who comes heie to the mad-house to see me, and out of compassion humours all Inv fancies. "I wonder how long they'll keep me here ? For- ever I hope. Until I get cured I'm sure! I hope they won't cure me. I vow I won't be cured. It's a great deal too pleasant to he mad, and I'll stay SO. I'll keep on calling myself Miss Black, and this mal-house my country seat, and the head- doctor my uncle, and the keepers servants until the end of time—so I will. Catch me coming to my senses when it's so delightful to be mad. I'm too sharp for that. I didn't grow up in Rag Alley, New York, for nothing." So, half in jest and half in earnest, Capitols soliloquised upon I-Er change of fortune. Her education was commenced, but progressed rather irregularly. Old Hurricazie boaght her books and rnarv, slates and copy-books, set her lessons in grammar, geography and history, and made her write copies, do sums, and read and recite lessons to him. Mrs. Condiment taught her the mysteries of cutting and basting, back-stitching and felling, hemming and seaming. A pupil as sharp as Capitols soon mastered her tasks, and sound herself each day with many hours of leisure, with which she did not know what to do.

These hours were at first occupied with exploring the old house, with all its attics, cuddles, cook- lofts and cellars; then In wandering through the old ornamental grounds, that were, even in winter and in total neglect, beautiful with their wild growth of evergreens; thence she extended her researches into the wild and picturesque country around,

She was never weary of admiring the great forest that climbed the heights of the mountain behind their house; the great bleak precipices of gray rocks seen through the leafless branches of the. trees; the rugged falling ground that lay before the house, and between it and the river; and the river itself, with its rushing stream and raging rapids. Capitols, had become a skilful as she had first been a fearless rider. Bat her rides were confined to the domain between the mountain range and the river; sbe was forbidden to ford the one or to climb the other. Perhaps if such a prohibition had never been made, Cap would never thought of doing the one or the other; but we all know the diabolical fascination there is in forbidden pleasures for young hnman nature. And no sooner had Cap been com- manded, if she valued her safety, not to cross the water or climb the precipice, than, as a natural consequence, she began to wonder what was in the valley behind the mountain, and what might be in the woods across the river! and she longed, above all things, to explore and find out for herself. She would eagerly have done so, notwithstanding the prohibition;• but Wool, who always attended her rides, was sadly in the way; if she could only get rid of Wool, she resolved to go upon a limited exploring expedition.
mats seen inrongti
of -the • I

- One day a golden opportunity occurred. It was a day of unusual beauty, when autumn seemed to be smiling upon the earth with her brightest smiles before passing away. In a word, it was Indian summer. The beauty of the weather had tempted Old Hurricane to ride to the county seat on particular business connected with his ward herself. Capitola, left alone, amusea herself with her tasks until the afternoon; then calling a boy, she ordered him to saddle her horse and bring him around. "My dear, what do you want with your horse? There is no onc to attend you; Wool has gone with his master," said Mrs. Condiment, as she met Capitola in the hall, habited for her ride. "I know that; but I cannot be mewed up here in the old house and deprived of my afternoon ride!" exclaimed Capitola, decidedly. "But, my dear, you must never think of riding out alone!" exclaimed the dismayed Mrs. Condi- ment. "Indeed I shall though I—and glad of the oppor- tunity!" added Cap, mentally. "But, my dear love, it is improper, imprudent, dangerous." "Why so?" asked Cap. "Good gracious, upon every account. Suppose you were to meet ruffians; suppose—oh, heaven ! suppose you were to meet with—BLACK DONALD I" "Mrs. Condiment, once for all do tell me who this terrible Black Donald is 7 Is he the evil one himself, or the Man in the Iron Mask, or the individual that struck Billy Patterson, or—who is he?" "Who is Black Donald? Good gracious, child, Ton ask me who is Black Donald?" II Yes—who is he? where is he? wnsm is he, that every cheek turns pale at the mention of his name?" asked Capitola. "Black Donald 1 Oh, my child, may you never know more of Black Donald than I can tell you. Black Donald is the chief of a band of ruthless desperadoes that infest these mountain roads, . robbing mail coaches, stealing negroes, breaking Into houses, and committing every sort of depreda- tion. Their hands are red with murder, and their souls black with darker crimes." "Darker crimes than murder " ejaculated Capitola. " Yes, child, yes—there are darker crimes! Only last wiater he and three of his gang broke into a solitary house where there was a lone woman and her daughter, and—it is not a story for you to hear, but if the people ha a caught Black Donald then, they would have burnt him at a stake. His life is forfeit by a hundred crimes. He is an outlaw, and a heavy price is set upon his head." "And can no one take him 7" "No, my dear; at least, no one has been able to do so yet. Ills very haunts are unknown, but are supposed to be in concealed mountain caverns." "How I would like the glory of capturing Black Donald!" said Capitola. "You, child—you capture Black Donald I You are crazy." "Oh, by stratagem I mean, not by force! Oh, how I should like to capture Black Donald 1— 'There's my horse. Good-bye 1" And, before Mrs. Condiment could raise another objection, Capitola ran out, sprang into her saddle, and was seen careering down the hill towards the river as fast as her. horse_oould

pulliiiiTup her Forse—tben, as bfe. sudlen she exclaimed, "I don't like this place either! it's right on the top of the bill so windy! and just see bow rocky the ground is! No! I'll not sit and rest here, and that I tell you 1" "I am afraid you are trifling with me, my pretty bird! take care! I'll not be trifled with 1" said the man.

"I don't know what you mean by trifling with you, any more than the dead. But I'll not sit down there on those sharp rocks, and so I tell you. If you will be civil and ride along with me until we get to the foot of the hill, I know a nice place, where we can sit down and have a good talk, and I will tell you all my travels, and you shall tell me all yours."

"Ex-actly—and where is that nice placer' _ "Why, in the valley at the foot of the hill." "Come! come on, then." " Slowly I slowly V' said Capitola—"l won't tire my horse." They rode over the hill, down the gradual descent, and on towards the centre of the valley. • They were now within a quarter of a mile of the river, on the opposite side of which was Hurricane Hall and—safety! The stranger drew rein, saying: "Come, my cuckoo! here we are at the bottom of the valley I now or never!" "Oh! now, of course! you see I keep my promise," answered Capitola, pulling up her horse. The man sprang from his saddle and came to her side.

"Please to be careful, now, don't let my riding skirt get hung in the stirrup," said Capitola, cautiously disengaging her drapery, rising in the saddle and giving the stranger her hand. In the act of jumping, she suddenly stopped and looked down, exclaiming: _ . .

"Good gracious I how very damp the ground is here in the bottom of the valley 1" "More objections, I suppose, my pretty one 1 but they won't serve you any longer. lam bent upon 'having a cosy chat with you, upon that very turf!" said the stranger, pointing to a little cleared space among the trees be.ide the path. "Now, don't be cross; just see how damp it is there; it would spoil my riding-dress, and give me my death of cold." • "Humph," said the stranger, looking at ker with a sly, grim, cruel resolve. "I'll tell you what it is," said Cap, "I'm not witty nor amusing, nor will it pay to sit out in the night air to hear me talk; but since you wish it, and since you were so good as to guard me through these woods, and since I promised, why, damp as it is, I will even get off and talk with you!" "That's my birdling." • "But hold on one minute. Is there nothing you • can get to put there for me to sit on—no stump, ' ror dry stone '' "No, my dear, I don't see any." Could you not turn your hat down and let me sit on that?"
" Ha, ha, hat why, your weight would crush it as flat as a flounder!"

"Oh 1 I know now!" exclaimed Capitols, with sudden delight. "You just spread your saddle cloth down there, and that will make a beautiful seat, and I'll sit and talk with you so nicely—only ' you must not want me to stay long, because if I don't get home soon I shall catch a scolding." "You shall neither catch a scolding nor a cold on my account, pretty one 1" said the man, going to his horse to get the saddle•cloth. "Oh, don't take off the saddle; i 1 will detain you too long," said Cap, impatiently. w "My pretty Cap, I cannot get te tloth without taking it off," said the man, beginning to unbuckle the girth.
" Oh, yes you can I you can draw it from under!" persisted Cap. "Impossible, my angel!" said the man, lifting off the saddle from his horse and laying it carefully by the roadside.

Then he toot off the gay, crimson saddle-cloth, and carried it into the little clearing and began carefully to spread it down. Now was Cap's time. Her horse had recovered from his fatigue. The stranger's horse was in the path before her. While the man's back was turned, she raised her riding-whip, and with a shout, gave the front horse a sharp lash that sent him galloping furiously ahead. Then instantaneously putting whip to her own horse, she started into a run.

Hearing the shout, the lush, and the starting of the horses, the b2filed villain turned and saw that his game was lost I He had been outwitted by a child I He gnashed his teeth and shook his fist in rage.
Turning, as she wheeled out of sight, Capitola —l'm sorry to ily—put her thumb to the side of her nose, and whirled her fingers into a semi-circle, in a gesture more expressive than elegant. _ _

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] AUNTIE. By the Author of "Gracie," "lii the Light of the Setting Sun," &o.
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.] AUNTIE. By the Author of "Gracie," "lii the Light of the Setting Sun," &o.

Tam is ray wedding gift to you, little: one: a bridal veil. Do you think it a strange pivesent to receive from an old maid? That veil was intended for me to wear at the altar; but I never wore it. Do you see what this is? It in a wedding dress. The delicate lace and muslin is torn; the gown is old-fashioned.

These faded flowers are one-blossoms. This withered wreath was to have crowned my hair when it was gold like yours. Now it is grey; the gold of my hair has faded with the bridal flowers. They have lain in. that drawer, with the dress and vol, for nearly thirty years. Only once in that time have I turned the key in the lock and looked at them—only once, until now. Then I Shed bitter tears over the aShes of my youth; now I do not weep. Time has ihealed the wound inflicted so long ago, but the scar remains; that can never disappear.

DZi'you wonder at my words, deans; wonder why that veil was never worn, why the lace of that dress is in shreds, why those orange-dowers like there—dead/ Shall I tell You, little one? Perhaps it will tire my restless Daisy to listen to an chi maid's otery. V•ou say not. Well, •if you care to hear it,, will keep you only a few minutes. I%romanee is short and matter-of•fact enough. Kneel at my feet in the firelight, little one. I like the gloaming and the firelight; it reminds me of the time when the sweetest happiness came to me, and wite.n the deepest sorrow darkened my life. Ah, it was a man's sin and a woman's pride that altered my life from one of ley to one of grief. It is nearly thirty years since that 'bridal gown was made., ;and those orange-blossoms gathered. I was young then; my face was fair and my hair golden—as yours is. Your auntie has not always been grey and sour. I have grown old; but I remember'it all as vividly as if it were only a little while ago. And it is thirty years:! I have found it hard to forget. As a girl, I was considered beautiful. It is no vanity to say it now that my beauty has gone. I do not think I was vain. Of course, I was proud of, thankful for, my fairness of face, for we like to be thought fair. I was called the belle of the county,and was an heiress into the bargain. My wealth 'brought me many lovers. But, dearie, I was of a hard, proud nature.; one who could not forgive a sin, however dear the sinner. Crime I could ,not understand. Had I not been nurtured in the midst of wealth and affluence, where there Was little temptation to sin? If I had been wiser anthelearer-sighted, and known how weak man is, how-strong the temptations placed before him, it might have been different. 'Often do I wish I had been more gentle and forgiving, • less cruel and harsh. But the lesson taught me was a severe one. I have never forgotten it. When I was twenty years old, I learned to love. Yes, dear, your old grey-haired, dim-eyed auntie has loved, even as you do now. She is an old maid ; maybe she is sour and unlovable, but she has loved and been loved. His name was Mark. He was not a handsome man; but he was gentle and winning. I seemed I.:otiose my heart to him ere.l was aware of it: and he loved me. He asked me to be his wife. He was poor, I was rich; what did that matter to me? I was glad to be 4alyle to take him wealth with my love. At first Lwondered whether he wooed me for my money:; • but he did not. Even now I, think he loved mess I loved him.

The wedding was arranged to take place just ,after my two-and-twentieth birthday. .Our engagement only lasted three months. My mother did hot believe in long engagements, and Mark elaid he wanted his wife. So the trousseau was 'ordered and great preparations were made. Two or three days before that on which the mar- riage was arranged to take place, the wedding dress came home. These it lies—old-fashioned and ugly; then, it was very pretty. Of course„l tried it on. I went downstairs to show them all. It .looked fresh and dainty, did that mass of white 'muslin and lace. One 'Amy sisters—your mother —said that it was unluoky.to wear the dress before the wedding-day. I langhed. What cloud could possibly darken the sunshine of my happiness? I went to the library to thaw my parents my finery. I found my mother in 'tears, my father looking
aye and croubled.. My new was forgotten—.

div.p: lents taken.
at my motherle; feet, -and put mi arms around her, begging of laor to tell me what grieved her.

She would not tell me. • " Take off your wedding .dress," she said. "Yogi must not wear it to- day." "But why are you crying ?" I asked. I turned to my father. " What is .the matter?" My parents looked at each other. Mother bowed her head, and father turned to me. "Read this," he said. _

I took the letter he held out to me, and read it through. At first, could not understand it. _After again reading every word, its meaning seemed to dawn upon me. It s.wastfrom Mark's uncle, and it said that he, my betrothed, had forged his uncle's name for a cheque to the amount of a thous- and pounds. What I said ado not remember. I fell at my mother's feet, and bowed my head on !her knee in shame and agony. " Oh ! Margaret, my child, what shall you do?" she whispered, brokenly. "Do ! ' I answered. "Learn the truth of him, •and then bid him farewell."

"Margaret, can you do that ! You love him— your heart will break." "My heart! My heart k dead ! And as for love, I cannot love a forger," was my reply. I sent my parents from me, and despatched a servant with a note to Mark, who lived a couple of miles away. I waited for him in the library. I threw myself lista a law arm-chair, and buned my face in its cushions. I had not removed my wedding dress; I never thought to do so. Little one, can you understand the misery I felt, on learning that my love was a forger?' Can you understand my resolve not to marry him if what that letter said was true? I, who was so proud of my 'untarnished name, who abhonred sin and revered honour, who had trusted and loved this man as I trusted my Maker—you will forgive me for being harsh and cruel if you understand my hatred of this despicable sin, and my pain when I found that the idol I had worshipped was made of meaner stall than even common clay.

Soon he came. The gloaming had fallen, and the light of the fire brightened the room, mingling with the cold moon- rays, which stole through the uncurtaincd windows. I arose as he came through the shadows to where the red fine-light fell upon his face, and showed so plainly the love in his eyes as they rested on roe, standing there in my white bridal gown. He put his arms around me, he drew me to his breast, and kissed me, murmuring soft, endearing words that ad my sorrow harder to bear. He called in( his dear love, his wife; he said how fair I was, how proud he felt of his darling, how he loved me. I tore myself from his arms, and told him all I knew of his crime. How well do I remember the change that passed over his face at my words !All the light and gladness disappeared ; he grew pale, and his eyes grew wistful. But he did not deny it. He was hard-pressed for money; his creditors were clamouring for their payments, and, in desperation, he forged his uncle's name to a stolen cheque. " Why did you not come to me?" I asked him. "I would have given you half my fortune—any- thing, rather than this disgrace." ".1 could not," he answered, "I should have been ashamed." "And are you not ashamed of this?" I said. 'Twould have been better to have humbled yourself to me, who loved you, than to degrade yourself by a mean, criminal sin. Oh, I trusted, loved you I and you have fallen to this ! " He knelt at my feet, and clutched the folds of my gown. ,But I wrenched it from him, tearing the delicate lace with my ruthless fingers. He prayed for pardon. "Margaret! my love! I sinned, but I have suffered." •
I told him wa must part. "Bus !" he cried. "But not for ever, you do not mean for ever, Margaret! Ah, no! that would be too cruel. And you are not cruel. You love me: vnn told me so."

div.head: EXAMINER, '-',ATIJIRDAY, DECEMBER 28 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, '-',ATIJIRDAY, DECEMBER 28 1895.

" rhatc you," Was my answer. "Di you think I could love a man who would stoop to sloth false. hood and deceit? Do you think I could iisulo the wife of one whom I could never trust ?, No ! You and I have done with each other. Les.ve me. Let us end an interview that can bring no happiness to either."

But he knelt there, pleading and imploring for pardon. He told me that it was the desperate act of a moment of madness, that he deeply repented. He Legged of me to "grant him a chance," to postpone the marriage until he had given me. proof of his truth and love. But I said to him, nay. I tore myself from him, never heeding how I spoilt the muslin and lace of my dress. I took from my finger the ring he had given me as a pledge of our betrothal, and threw it at his feet. I was angry— I loathed him for his sin. I sent him from me. He wept on the ground before me, and entreated, prayed for mercy; but I sent him from me. My heart was harder than steel.

And when he was gone—for ever—l fell on the floor in all my torn finery, and cried in my passion- ate and angry sorry, I did not see Mark again. They told me that his uncle did not prosecute him; but he disowned him and sent him into the world, refusing ever to see his face again. Where he had gone no one knew. He had never been seen since the day on which his uncle cast him off. The forgery was committed three months before that which was to be our wedding-day, just before he asked me to be his wife.

[locked my bridal dress and veil with the bright, pretty orange-blossoms in that drawer. I put the key in my desk, and never looked at it again for years. Seven years passed. I was still unwedded. During that time, I had an offer of marriage, which was refused. I kept out of society. My heart was broken. Society was no place for me. I was nine-and-twenty years of age, when my father came to me, and said: " Margaret, will you come with me?' "To where?"

"Put on your hat, and I will show 'yom" I obeyed him, wonderingly. lie took .me into a cab. We drove into one of the commonest, most miserable parts of the East filnd of London. We stopped in the middle of a street that seemed to be a mass of great, close, tuMble- down houses. It was a no'isy, horrible place, full of filthy, half-naked 'children, aud men and women as filthy as the children. A girl was lolling against the doorpost of the 'house we entered; her eyes well() bloodshot and her face flushed. She laughed and ieered at me when she caught sight of lite in my rich clothes. I passed her with a shudder, for I realised the horrible fact that this girl—a mere child—was drunk "Father, where have ,you brought site?" I whispered. "Follow use closely. You .are quite safe," he replied. . , He led me up a ricketty staircase. Here and there on the broken handrail were treoes of old. fashioned carving, exquisitely wrought, that told that this fearful place was once the home of the rich and great, that dainty feet and sillesn draperies had swept down these Totten stairs, feet that had decayed like the beauties of this house, and were horrible now like this. The :place ,resounded with the oaths and shrieks of men :and women and chil- dren; and once, perhaps, love mows had been , whispered here; the dow, 'sweet laughter of women and the flatteries 'of .covaliers had echoed softly in the dint galleries—new so filthy, .so loathsome. We encountered children on, the way, sometimes noisy women. Once an old man passed us with slouching gait and bent head, and I thought to myself how many limes were lost in something far worse than death in these horrible ,London dens.

My father knocked at a door at the top of the house. We entered a low-ceiled squalid garret, destitute of furniture. He crossed softly to a 113.-1 in one corner of the ,miserable room. I call it a bed, but it was merely a heap of rags. He beckoned to me to follow him. I did so.

I looked down, and saw the form of a man lying there rigid and motionless. Illooked at the pale, still face, and recognised my lover, my Mark: he lay dead at my feet. Ibis of no use to attempt to describe my misery. Ife whom I loved, whom I had parted from-manger, layaiieless in a wretched garret ! When he left bis uncle he had striven to earn his living by many ways, and at last had resorted to his pen. The result was death from starvation —death in a garret for my darling, who had been a king amongst men. I shuddered to think that my Mark had ever lived in the midst of these drunken men And -women. 'Surely he was well punished for his-sin. But it was over now, and he was dead. _ . _ _ _

When I went home again, I took the key from the desk and opened that drawer. There lay the torn wedding ,clothes and ywithered flowers. I wept many hitter tears over them. All my cruelty to my erring love came back to me, and I prayed that my harshness might be ,pardoned. When my sorrow was spetrt, I locked.the drawer again, and have never opened it since until now.

I may be wrong, but it always seems to me that I murdered him, that if I had not been so hard to him, if I had been gentle.and kind, if 1 had given him a chance—anything—anything—so that I had not sent him from me he would have lived and still have loved me. Perhaps, after all, it is as well as it is: God knows best. I have endeavoured to resign myself to Heaven's will. And yet—there is always " and yet," little ,one. ee this portrait; this is your old Auntie when she was a gird. We found it in his hand as he lay dead, and it makes me think that he loved me to the end, even though I .wa,s cruel and unforgiving. This is a portrait of Mark. You see, Daisy, he was not co handsome as your lover is; but his was a kindly, gentle face; and I loved him. You say you do not think it looks the face of a man who would stoop le crhne. No, Daisy, no; but his up- bringing was bad, and his temptation was great. Ah, I can find exouses for kiln now; I could find none then. Here are a few letters which he wrote to me during our short engagement,.and a little bunch of faded flowers; he gave them to me on the day he asked me to be his wife. I have often read the letters and kissed the flowers and wept over them. I read them now, but do net weep; I only pray that his sin may be forgiven, and my cruelty par- doned, and that when death takes me from this world, I may go to my dear one, and find rest and peace and love after all I have endured. Sometimes, when you are singing in the twilight, I close my eyes and imagine that it is your mother's voice I hear. My thoughts wander to the past, when she used to sing to us as We sat in the gleam- ing7-he and I—dreaming -dreams that were never realised.

Soon after his death a good man sought me for his wife ' • but vainly. I knew that the memory of my dear dead oae would never leave me, and that my life would be lived in the hope of meeting him in the great hereafter. And when .I looked into the face of my living lover, the ghost of the dead one seemed to rise between us. I refused. him. He has since married a fair young_ wife, awl I believe they are very happy together. Soon after you were born, I came to live with your mother, and have never left her. She knows my story, but she never speaks of it. It i 3 better not. . Now, you know why 'this Wedding-gown is crushed and torn, why this veil hever adorned a bride's head, why Auntie has never married. I have faded with the bridal flowers, but my love for the dead man is as strong as it was when I was young.and fair. But it was a different kind of love. I used to weep over his grave, but though I very often go and lay fair flowers there, I only pray that our sins may be forgiven and we may soon meet again., I have told you my story, little one. You are the only one to whom I have spoken of it for over twenty years. Wear this bridal veil, and remem- ber, dear, that it is hest to be gentle and kind to those who are sinful. Never speak a harsh word when it is as well to speak a gentle one.

It is for this reason that an assertion like the follow sticks up above the dead level at our stupid talk, and becomes noticeable : " When I saw how pale I had grown I said to myself, it was because something had gone out of my blood."
There! that is a statement with the seeds of an idea in it. Suppose we follow it up by quoting the rest of the letter which contains it.

In December, 1890, says the writer, " I fell into a poor state of health. I was tired, languid, and weary without any apparent cause. My appetite left me, and all food, even the lightest and simplest kinds, caused me great pain in the chest and stomach. When I saw how pale I had grown I said to myself it was because some- thing had gone out of my blood.

"Then my sleep was broken, and night after night I scarcely closed my eyes. It wasn't long before I became so weak and dejected that I took no interest in things around me. I was so nervous that common sounds annoyed and worried me: even the noises made by my own children in their talk and at their play. " There was a disgusting taste in my mouth ; it mad, me sick, and often gave me a shivering sensation all over. When I saw others eating and enjoying their meals I felt as though it were a strange thing; h a way / wondered how they could do it. For myself I could eat hardly anything. Food went against me, and I turned away from it, as one turns from smells or sights that are offensive. And yet I knew, what everyone knows, that withot t sufficient food the body languishes and weakens. And such was the case with ins as month after month went by.

"During all this time, so full of pain aud discourage- ment, I was attended by a docter who did what he could to relieve me, but without success. I do not say he did not understand my complaint for may he not have understood it without having the weans of curing it ? "

The answer to the lady's question : Yes, easily enough. All intelligent studious doctors " understand" consumption,cholera, cancer, &c„ without (as yet) hav- ing the means of curing them. There is usually a wide gap between the dig covery of a want and the way to supply it. " I will now," continues the letter," tell you kow came to be cured. In April, 1891, 1 read in a email book or pamphlet about Mother Seigel's Syrup. The book said the Syrup was a certain remedy for all diseases of the stomach, indigestion in every form, and dyspepsia ; and it also said that most of the complaints we suffer from are caused by that. On looking ,over the symp- toms described inl the book, and comparing them witk my own, I saw plainly that my ailment was dyspepsia. "We sent inammediately for a bottle of this medicine- and after taking it a few days I began to feel better. In a very short time, by keeping on with the Syrup accord- ing to the directions, I could eat without pain or dig- ' tress, and digest my food. I also slept soundly and naturally. Then my strength came back and with it the colour to my face. In short, after a few weeks use of Mother Seigef's Syrup, I was hearty and strong as ever. And I should be indeed ungrateful If I were not willing that others should have the benefit of my experi- ence. You are therefore free to; print my letter if you think it will be useful. (Signed) (Mrs.) M. Truran, Marton, Lincoln, April 24, 1895.

I simply desire to say to Mrs. Truran that her idea about the blood is a perfectly correct one, All our food (the digestible part of it) is turned into blood, and in that shape it feeds the entire body. When the blood gets thin and poor <lacking in nourishment), we lose flesh and grow feeble and pale. And the casts' of the blood getting thin and poor isindigestion, or dyB7epBia. How easy this is to understand when once you get hold of the right end of it. Mother Seigel's Syrup has the peculiar power to correct what is wrong about the digestion,and thus enables the digestive machinery to make good rich blood, which is life and health and beauty.

div.head: DROWNING FATALITY AT LA.TCHFORD LOCKE.
div.p: THE DROWNING FATALITY AT LA.TCHFORD LOCKE.

The inquest upon the body of John Hankey, who was drowned in the Manchester Ship Canal on Saturday morning, took place at the residence of the deceased's parents, Ship Canal View., Latchford. Themes Hankey stated that the ' deceased was his brother, and was 2.9 years of ago. He .(witness) started from his home shortly before six o'clock on the previous merning,in company with the unfortunate young man, with the purpose of going to their work at Messrs. Pierpoint's tan yard,situated on the opposite side of the Ship Canal. In order to get there .quickly they had been in the habit of crossing overthe lock gates to gain the other side of the waterway instead of going the longer route by way of the swing bridge. On Friday morning they had crossed one lock in safety, although the fog was so dense that the top of the water was not discernible. Witness turned back with the intention of procuring a lamp, but did not say anything to his brother. Having got the lamp he returned, and when near the spot where he left the deceased be heard a splash, lie called for help, and after staying a short time he went to Meseta. Pierpoint's to make certain whether his brother had arrived. Having ascertained that deceased had not turned up at the works ha re- turned to the locks, and found that the body had been recovered. Every assistance was rendered by the lock- keepers. William Jones, lock gateman, said that on the pre- vious morning be was on duty at the locks when about six o'clock he heard a shout. He called for the electric light to be turned on,and this having been ,done he pro- ceeded to the spot with the grappling irons. He re- covered the body 40 minutes later fromabout.4s feet of water. There were no bruises on the body, and ho,with others,tried artificial respiration,but without avail. The deceased would have had a fall of about six feet to the water. At the time of the occurrence there were seve- ral steamers in the locks which bad been moored there until the fog lifted sufficiently to allow them to proceed en their journey, and deceased might probably have slipped over one of the ropes by which they were fas- tened.

It -Was explained by a representative of the Canal Company that the road over the locks was a public one. As required by the Act there had to be a safe footway across the waterway. A short discussion then took place, several of the jurymen remarking that the lighting of the locks was inadequate at the time of the accklent. A verdict was eventually returned of " Accidentally drowned," and the jury suggested that the Ship Canal Company be approached with reference to the lighting of the locks during dark and misty weather.

div.head: SHIP CAN AL
div.p: SHIP CAN AL
LIST WEEK'S TRAFFIC.

Notwithstanding the dense flg which on Friday com- pletely suspended the navigation of the Ship Canal, last week's traffic was the heaviest recorded since the Am week of September. During the seven days ended Fri- day,. December 20, 135 seagoing vessels, with an aggre- gate net registered tonnage of 47,000 tons, arrived at and sailed from the various docks, wharves, &c., of thr waterway—an increase of 24 vessels and 13,109 tons on the traffic during the preceding, week. fhe coastwiee trade was rePr•sented by 98 ships of 21,203 tons,against 87 ships of 20.118 tons ; and the foreign traffic by 37 ships of 25,797 tons, against 2t ships of 15,380 tons in the previous seven days, the arrivals from foreign port: being the largest on record. Unusual activity war manifested in the Baltic and Spanish fruit trades. Six steamers entered with timber, wood pulp, awl general cargo from Scandinavia. Denmark, and the Baltic ; nearly 14,000 bales of cotton arrived from Alexandria and Galveston ; between 35,000 and 40,800 eases of green fruit were discharged by the steamers Fez, Heimdahl, Alert, and Allot's° from Valencia, Eifrida from Seville, and Danish Prince from Jaffa ; and a consignment of bauxite was received from Cette Amongst other cargoes imported were one of timber from Canada, seven of pig iron, eight of china clay. seventeen of various kinds of stone and slate from Wales, and sixteen general cargoes from Hamburg. Syria, Rotterdam, New York, Treport, Antwerp, Rouen, Leith, Glasgow, London, and Bristol. Two cargoes i! coal were exported ,one of pitch ,and seventeen of genera: ! merchandise. The traffic this week is expected to be ' below the average, as wark at the Manchester and Ha', ford docks, and at Runcorn and Saltport will be sue- ! pended on Wednesday and Thursday—Christmas Das and Boxing Pay,—except by special arraagement.

div.p: "CAPITAL", CITAI

. The announcement that China has granted to Ru•sia a naval station at Kiao Chow has fallen very fiat in the present preoccupied state of the public mind, already sufficiently engrossed with the Vene- zuelan dispute. In reality, it is a mere transference of the Russian winter station from Nagasaki, in Japan, to the Chinese coast. Thus Rus,ia secures greater freedom, and better accommodation for her , ships and stores, than she enjoyed at Nagasaki; and, on the other hand, China detaches Russia more , completely from her old enemy, and draws the ' bonds of friendship a little more close between Russia and herself. The station at Nagasaki was rendered necessary by the ice-bound condition of the Russian ports during winter, and the desire for one accessible at all times of the year is natural on the part of a great Power, however much it may excite the Silomos of politics. It has to be noted that it is a mere right to the use of the port which China makes over, with the permission to construct warehouses or stores on shore. It involves no ces- sion of territory to Russia, and no right on the part of that Power to turn it into a fortified position.

One consequence the Anglo-American episode is expected to have is that the defences of Canada will receive more attention both in the Dominion and at home than they have received quite lately. It is clear that if other Administrations at Washington take the same view of the rights and duties of the United States under the Monroe Doc- trine no country having territory in North or South America (to which the West Indian Islands and Hawaii, if not Samoa, are to be added) is safe, and as Canada is our most vulnerable point in case of dispute, the protection of the Dominion will, I am told, be the subject of careful consideration from the military and naval authorities. lam also able to say that the attitude of the Canadian Govern- ment and people during the crisis has caused the utmost satisfaction in the official world here. The talk in the United States,even by sensible men like Mr. Depew, about the conquest of Canada has, I am assured on very good authority,done more to check the party in the Dominion which favours in a more or less speculative fashion annexation to the Re- than any amount of argument. The Canad- ians deeply resent this contemptuous talk of con- quest and annexation as if they were the inhabi- tants of a small West annexation, island,to be treated as their masters at Washington choose. So perhaps the episode may not be without a beneffcial effect on the cohesion and loyalty of the parts of the British Empire to the whole.

Writing in the January number of the" Church Monthly" on his favourite game, Dr. Grace recom- mends cricket to the working classes as tlae most educational of open-air pastimes. It has about it " a glorious uncertainty," which " will very soon teach a player not to be selfish or conceited." While " professir,nalism, as a rule, means in all kinds of sport,gamblingt cricket," though it has a greater number of professional players to-day than at any time in its history, is above suspicion in that respect." One thing "W. G." is sorry to see, and that is "the great increase in League and cup matches. This is making too much of a business of the game, and leads to no end of disputes and quarrels,which did not occur when clubs were play- ing merely a friendly match with a neighbouring club. It is to be feared that it may encourage gambling, which it is hoped will never be associ- ated with our noble game."

According to the gossip of the military clubs, the Duke of Cambridge's retiring pension is not to be very large. It will not exceed, it is said, £l,OOO. There would be great opposition from Radical quarters to he voting of such an amount as proba- bly the Government would like to give him, and were the pension on a very liberal scale, the discus- sion, in all likelihood, would have to be closure& This would not be agreeable either to the Govern- ment or the duke. His Royal Highness enjoys a re- tiring allowance as honorary colonel of the Grena- dier Guards, and as he retires under the old rules it is much greater than Lord Wolseley will receive when he retires under the new.

In addition to the baron of beef,the royal kitchens at Windsor have during the past week been busily engaged in preparing an enormous plum pudding, or rather some twenty or thirty puddings made out of the same compound of some thirty to forty pounds of savory materials. It is the Queen's habit to send a pudding to each of her posterity in time for Christmas Day, and so the cooking has to be advanced in order that time may be allowed for some lengthy journeys. The puddings are none the worse for travelling. As a matter of fact, they will keep for nearly a year and improve by keeping, while it seems as if they could never have too much cooking. One of the " points " of the royal pudding is the inclusion of candied cherries.

By whatever process it may have been accom plished, it is beyond doubt that nothing has more deeply burned into the convictions of the advanced Labour party here than the belief that President Cleveland's first message is the result of a deep-laid plan for distracting the attention of the American people from the labour question to foreign politics. It would take a great deal of proof to convince the English people generally that this is the case; but there is no doubt that Mr. Keit Hardie's speech the other night expresses the view the extreme Labour school of politicians here take of the American crisis. The result is that they find themselves, for once in their lives,ranged on the side of the British Government, and that is something really worth chronicling. It is probable that American sym- pathy with the Republican forms of government in South America, the belief that Great Britain is bullying Venezuela,the supposed rights of American concesgionaries in the gold-bearing region under dispute.and an electioneering manouvre, have more to d, with the issue of the belligerent message than 1 the labour question in Chicago. The economic disasters which the message has already created are much more likely to strengthen the disaffected party and the Labour party than to turn aside the attention of the nation from the labour problem, and if war were really to break out it would spread economic ruin from one end of the States to the other.

Some people are born with a wonderful head for finance. Mr. Robinson, of Dudley Ifouse,is a strik- ing instance. He paid some .£6,000 for the Lang- laagte property and it is now valued at .£300,000, He paid £7,000 for the Randfontein Estate, and it is now valued at .£600,000.

I hear that in all probability the Wesleyan Metho- dist Conference will hold its sessions during the ensuing three years in the North of England. Fol- lowing Liverpool, it was hoped that York would be in 1897 the conference centre, but difficulties have arisen, and the negotiations are likely to fall through. Such being the case, private information says that the Methodists of the West Hiding are prepared to renew the hospitality of thirteen years I ago, when the Conference met in Leeds.

Lord Dufferin has been much gratified by the compliment which the French Canadians have just paid him. If there is one spot in their historic city of Quebec,of which an French Canadians are proud, it is the magnificent promenade on the heights naar which Wolfe and Montcalm met in the last terrible encounter between France and England in the New World. The view from this promenade up and down the St. Lawrence is one of the finest in the world. It has now received the official title of 'Dufferin Terrace," in recognition of the kindly feelings which Lord and Lady Dufferin evoked among the French Canadians while resident in Canada. In acknowledging the compliment Lord Dufferin promises to cherish " the precious docu- ment" as a heirloom at. Clandeboye.

Tuesday night was a "record " Christmas-eve. here in the way of weather. Chill rain, biting blasts, in which no umbrella could "live," streets that were simply rivers of mire, showers of mud hot up by the ceaseless heavy traffic—all these awaited those who, on business or pleasure bent, leserted the fireside for the open air. Yet in spite of it all the Christmas belle rang out on crowds determined to be cheerful under the most depress- ing conditions. Multitudes pouring out of the theatres met others bound for midnight services in the churches, and belated postmen still deliver- ing their burdens on the stroke of midnight mingled with the throng. " Midnight Masses," whether Anglican or Roman, are, I am inclined to think, more general than they were five years ago. 11 Cardinal Vsughatt seems to have withdrawn the !strict prohibition of his predecessor against, the ' time-honoured practice, although admission to Roman Catholic churches is still by ticket only. Those who went to their midnight Mass this year (nay be said to have obtained "a heroic decree " of devotion, for the weather,which was not sofficently disagreeable to deter them from a re;igious observ- nee, was quite bad enough to clear the streets of oysterers' as the worshippers happily found on .reaving church for home in the small bours.j

Mr. Edison has been telling an interviewer terrible things about what electricity can do in war. It is pitiful to hear a clever man talking nonsense about what he does not understand. When he first proposed a couple of years ago to destroy an enemy by pumping "electrified " water over him, another American electrician remarked, " I should just put on a wet rubber coat with a long skirt to it, and let Mr. Edison pump away at me till he was tired." The electrified wire as a de- fence to a fortress was actually tried by the Austrians at Komorn during the fortress manceuvres not long ago. The story goes that a wire entangle- ment was connected with a powerful dynamo, and a flock of sheep was driver upon the wires. A few were killed, but the rest survived, most of the ,1 current apparently going to earth through the bodies of the first victims. Electricity has, of ' course, its recognised place in war, but it does other and more valuable work than Mr. Edison assigned to it in his talk with the reporter.

div.head: BETTING MAN'S "AMATEUR."
div.p: A BETTING MAN'S "AMATEUR."

CONFESSION OF FRAUDS BY A CYCLIST. (From" The Cyclers' News.") " Thank Heaven, my racing days are over ! Hence- forth I will endeavour to be true to myself and the world. Gone for ever are the days of fraud, deceit, and hypo- crisy !" To hear a well-known amateur thus deliver himself surprised me. Knowing him intimately, I felt con- strained to ask tt e connection between his racing career and "fraud, deceit and hypocrisy," I "Promise to keep my name a secret,and I will tell all. You may afterwards think ill of me, but confessing to a friend will do me good." The necessary promise was given, our pipes recharged, and glasses refilled ; then, after looking at me for a moment as though estimating the effect his story would have upon me, he started to tell, or rather confess, many compromising incidents in his career upon the path. "When I became of age, I got a bit of money, and as that stuff burns holes In my pockets,it soon went. One of the articles I got in exchange was an ordinary bicycle Winning a club race fired me with ambition, and soon I was practising upon a well-known track in the Midlands. My first machine was very light for a roadster. Upon it I won a couple of open mile races from 130 and 100 yards respectively. In the latter race the scratch man caught me 50 yards from home, but he was run out, and I, having a bit up my sleeve, got the verdict by a length and came in for quite an ovation. A day or so after a gentleman in the trade congratulated me upon the good fight I had made with the scratch man, and offered to lend me a racing machine. I tried his machine, and a few spins convinced me that weight told, for soon Icould hold my own in practice with the 50 yards men. At the next meeting I was allotted 90 yards in themile and 165 yards in the two miles. Won both heats comfortably, and felt sure of bringing off the double event. Upon turning out for the mile final,a man approached and offered me £lO not to try. With scant ceremony he was told to 'get,' and a similar answer was given to a fellow-competitor who had taken the precau- I tiou to pledge me to secrecy. Not knowing that he was going to ask me to do anything wrong, I had promised to keep the conversation strictly private. The race needs little description. The limit men were soon caught,and I took the lead,hut lost it just as the bell rang. The two men who had sprinted by could not keep up their spurt, and it was evident they were at my mercy ; but try as I would, I could not get past, and judge of my horror when I discovered they were purposely riding wide to shut me out I I shouted Inside I inside as loudly as I could. To no purpose, however. The narrow tr ck aided them, and but for the outside man sitting up in the straight, I should not have got second. Upon dis- mounting,l laid an objection against the winner. It was overruled,and ten shillings deposit was forfeited. In the two miles I went clean away from the field, and won by 30 yards. Result : I was hauled up before the union and asked to explain my riding. Uponrepudiating any connection with betting or betting men, I was let off with a caution. This specimen of the union justice made my blood boil. Elence-1 forth I must go in the swim or get pocketed, robbed, and insulted. I chose the former course, prac- tically made cycle racing my business, and was soon known as a ' thick un.' Gradually I sank,until I never thought anything of going to a meeting with a couple of bookmakers, and was ready to lose whenever the ' hook' required such a proceeding to keep the balance on the right side. A good man is never seen talking to persons of the 'layer of odds' persuasion. All that bud- ness is done through the trainer, or more often by a friend who enters one event merely for the sake of get- ting a pass to the dressing room. • "Besides,what I made by betting,l was paid to ride the machines ; got something for most of the testimonials I gave; occasionally received ameunts of £2 to £8 from hon. secs. of sports who wish to secure my entry,and ad- vertise me to be a certain starter for their show ' • and, latterly,from tyre companies. Many of the prizes I have won are not worth one-third the advertised value, but considering I got so much in hard cash to attend the meetings where these sports were put up I cannot com- plain. " When the N.C.U. made the payment of entrance fees compulsory, certain sports secretaries took to enclosing stamps and postal-orders with entry form. A nice way of carrying out the law, especially when I say the hon. secretary in more cases than one was an official of the local centre of the N.C.U. Back-markers, above suspic- ion, consider it perfectly legitimate to arrange which race each shall go for, and assist each other by pacing accordingly. I remember once making such a bargain with a very smart handicap rider. It was at a meeting in Lancashire, where two events appeared to be in our hands. Be was to win the first race and myself the second. He won very cleverly, and raked in a few shekels. The second race was the three-mile handicap, and we paced and paced about until every one was caught a couple of laps from the finish. When it came to sprinting there were only we two in it, and I appeared to have a dead cert., but instead of being a non-trier, my fellow conspirator came with a wet sail and won on the spot. Considsring he had backed him- self for both events, his apologies and explanations did not go far with me. However, he thought that I, like others whom be had treated in a similar manner, would not retaliate. Two years later, I met him at a meeting where we both figured as entrants for a very valuable pot—ene of those to-be,-won-three-times trophies. He had won it twice already, and was desirous of making it his own property. The promoters of the sports were equally anxious he should not, and, in addition to giving an extra prize to any other than the man who had two shares in it, they paid my expenses and five pounds to knock him out. He knew who had the hest chance.and tried to buy MP Out. I refused to consider anything under ten pounds in cash. prepaid. After a lot of haggling he paid ten pounds to me, and then lost the race. I entered a dark-horse—a young rider I could trust, and who was destined to become a champion. We had a fortnight's training together, and I felt certain he could heat the holder of this big pot. Mr. Darkhorse won, and 'cleared with bets and one thing and another over fifty pounds at that meeting. I once nearly Ent done at Grimsby for roping; it was my first visit to town, and the handicapper had dealt very liberally with me. I won two heats, but did not get placed in the finals. The fishermen tumbled over one another to get to my bookmakers who were laying 6 to 4 against me. The other pencillors barred me. Some one at the gather- ing reported tile to the N.C.U., hut nothing definite be- came of it, so I went on in the old, sweet way. " You will.no doubt,thiek me a scoundrel for showing you the tricks of the trade now I have retired, but rest I assured the amateurs who to-day are receiving money for machines or tyres are safer than ever from detection, and so long as two people are wilt- ing to conspire together so long will the N.C.U. he powerless to enforce an ideal state of amateurism. Just as N.C.U. officials utilise their position for advertis- ing or other business proposes when possible, so does the 'cote racing man keep an ere to the main chance. You may hardly credit it, hut the N.C.U. official once . aecempanied me on a week's racing tour, and accepted his share of the profits. He afterwards spent a couple of day,' at my house and wrote several gushing articles about the pure state of my amateurism. All bosh ! Every good man lea wrong 'un according to the present ama- tour definition. Whether he be a path or road champion it matters little. I have never done any road racing,but the money I have received for pacing on the road is suffieient to tell MA that road riders are not mugs. Re- cords Cost a lot, and are worth a lot teo. But I see you are yawning—enough ? I have finished ; SOMA other time I will tell you a few eye-openers about time keepers, judges and sport offieials generally." We sat for a time in silence. I had no comments to offer, and when I left him it was to dot down as much SS I could remember of his recital, carefully eliminating names, dates, and places.

div.head: GAS OF THE FUTURE.
div.p: THE GAS OF THE FUTURE.

The gas we burn has says '6 General Sittings," many serious drawbacks. It is hoped that the latest illumin- ant, acetylene, will largely lake its place in the future. Acetylene turns with a brilliant light and can now be obtained from what is practically a waste product— carbide of calcium, a crystalline body which, when treated with water, yields acetylene almost quite Pure. The gas which is thus obtained has a distinct garlic- like odour, so that its presence in air. due to leakage of pipes, would easily be perceived. During combustion it produces less heat than coal gas, less moisture, and less carbonic acid, and uses up about half the quantity of oxygen. The light is white, and for the same volume yields niueteen times as !Pilch radiance as coal can with an ordinary burner. Dr. Netter, who has published a rote on the subject in the Revue d'Hygiene," be. Heves that acetylene thus produced has a considerable future, since the ease and simple appliances with which it mar is, mitcle will render it suitable for use for small installations. Further, its addition in certain proportions to ordinary coal gas will increase very much its illuminating power.
