div.head: WINTER.
div.p: WINTER.

In sombre clouds around him piled Old Winter hides his rugged form ; And, bent on pleasure grand and wild, He rides upon the rolling storm. The earth is stripped where'er he ties, The forests moan beneath his roar; And tumbling waves before him rise, And toss their wreckage on the shore. Yet stern and savage though he be, And devastating in his ways' Some bright and kindly moods has he To cheer the dismal nights and days. For in his wildest, darkest bouts There are brief intervals of calm ; Some bursts of sunshine through the showers, And zephyrs sat as holy psalm. And then some shiv'ring, lonely bird, Sad remnant of the leathered throng ; With heart like curs, all grateful stirred, Will warble forth a cheesy song. How beautiful the rural scene, Calm resting in the virgin snow, When o'er it, from a sky serene, The sun pours down a golden glow I When night's dark clouds are backward rolled. And waiting heaven and earth are still ; What starry wonders then unfold. What glory gleams on vale and hill I And while we gaze some planet fair With light more lovely than the rest, Slow moving through the fields of air, Will fill the mind with visions blest. For such a star o'er Salem shed A guiding light of heavenly ray; When in his cheerless manger bed The infant "man of sorrows " And thoughts of Him should surely move Our pity for the pcor and sad; They need our help, they need our love, And these can make them rich and glad. Then let us care for young and old, For all our kindred in distress ; Be ours to shield them from the cold. And make their wants and sorrows less. J. Fl. W. CLINDINNING.

div.head: HORSELESS VEHICLES AND SANITATION.
div.p: HORSELESS VEHICLES AND SANI- TATION.

Looking at horseless carriages from the point of sani- tation, the " Lancet " says :—There can be no doubt that, as regards this important matter, the equine me- chanism is somewhat lacking. Our stables without the horse would be as pure as our homes if we were our- selves visible only as figures of still life, waxen or ivory models. The stablepit filled with the defiled bedding of our obedient and faithful four-legged servant would be known no more to our senses. The c-intagia bred in its midst and scattered in the dry dust of the summer air, to find their way within our sleeping and sitting rooms would be only the remembered signs of a past and primitive civilisation. The germs of glander would not tvirber and be hatched, as they still occasionally are, in the stalls of overcrowded mews. Thus far the margin of profit is on the side of him cho charges his vehicle with bteam or electric energy. Possibly unaccustomed evils wait for him also, for accidents will happen, even with machinery.

At the London Sessions en Saturday the trial ci Ed- ward Gray and George Barrett on charges in cenaection With the recent great robbery of silver ingots Irma Midland Railway van, was concluded. Barrett was sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude and three years' police supervision, and Gray to ei7hteen mouths' hard labour.

Such was the subject of a celebrated sermon preached irt Manehester.but the more practical problem of the day is how to make life worth living on earth. One of the important tri- butaries of the river of happiness is the possession of a com- fortable home. A home made bright and cheerful not only by the kind and loving dispositions of those living there, but made attractive by the good taste displayed in the furnishing. Furnishing is a very important factor in the matter of con- tinued self-satisfaction. Bo much jerry new London furniture is being now retailed by drapers that one needs to pause be-. fore rushing impetuously into the first draper's because of a cheap red ticket. High-class makers, such as Lan:WA:Enos:os, and Garnett,still exist, to whom the wealthy can still go with a long puree but to most people this would be a too expensive experiment. Again, the average man nowadays has a strong liking for a bargain ; anything obtainable at about half or quarter the cost has a strong fascination f r him. Is it possi- ble to obtain such an advantage in furnishing P Yes, and more than possible, it is an absolute fact. We cannot do better than recommend a visit to MR. WORSLEY'd FUR- NISHING PANTHEON, GAYTHORN. MANCHESTER.

r FHB Successful Establishment of any of the large ware- houses of Manchester is always of interest to the citizens. One of the most brilliant examples of the value of perseverance, enterprise, and tact is the now busy hive of Industry so well known as The Pantheon, which occupies 'such a prominent position in Gaythorn, near the Central , Station, Manchester. The building is a massive pile of f modern design, 150 feet long, six storeys high, with show - ,:room accommodation covering an area of over one million rsquare feet. The plate-glass windows are each 12 feet square. each square if broken costing nearly £3O to replace. Ten of 'these immense show windows form a portion of the frontage- e•This will give a faint idea of "The Pantheon" in outward appearance, but ah t—here pen fails altogether in attempting to do justice to anything like an adequate desoription of the Interior. "The Pantheon" was specially built to give the largest and most convenient floor space for showrooms, and cost £28,000, the floors specially constructed to carry enormous weight. To-day it stands as one of the smartest furnishing houses in Eneand, containing by far the largest and most comprehensive stock of any two houses In this large city; From basement to roof, from floor to ceiling, 'The Pantheon filled to overflowing with thousands of well bought, care- fully selected bargains, to attempt description of which would teas futile as Liverpool attempting to crush THE MANCHESTER %RIP CANAL. .rhe destinies of '• The Pantheon," are c ,utrolled and pre- sided over by its sole absolute proprietor, Mr. W. H. Worsley, whose sole study is an ever increasing desire to satisfy and please the thousands of customers who daily patronise and support his efforts. We invite the reader to accompany us in an imaginary visit to "The Pantheon' to see what it con- tains and how it is managed. On arrival we are at once strualc with the magnificent STARTLING APPEARANCE

of " The Great Pantheon," the immense long line of stupen- dous show windows displaying for sale capital specimens of high-class Second hand Furniture oy high-class makers, the sale of which has made "The Pantheon " famous.

UPON ENTERING THE BUILDING we see, at once that as far as stock is concerned there is sufficient furniture for nearly the whole of Manchester. We see at once visitors walking round inspecting from Oldham. Bolton. Bury, Bun: ley, Bleclrburn,Bacup. Rochdale, Preston. Warrington and all parts of Lancashire and Yorkshire, Cheshire, the Potteries. Wales, Sm. It is tbe cardinal rule of " The Pantheon " to give the fullest facilities for inepee- lion without feeling compelled to buy. The ground hoot is filled with the large specimens of bedroom furniture suitable for I.rge rooms ; we are told the smaller suites are on the top floor, to which we can travel by means of the hoist, or walk. Bedroom suites on the ground floor we notice by Lamb. original oost £l5O, price £35 ; by Goodall, cost £lBO, for £5O ;by Henry Ogden. cost £2OO, for £55. These are among the best suites, but one that strikes us with special attention is a fine handsome Bedroom Suite by Behan. in solid American walnut, heavily carved in bas relief, with large wardrobe fitted with brilliant crystal bevel mirrors dressing table unique with neatly fitted jewel drawers, env' mounted by large swing dressing glass ; washstand fitted with statuary marble and shaving mirror. thr, e chairs. pedestal table de nuit, and towel horse •, what originally cost £6O you can obtain for £25. Over 200 bedroom Suit'es are in stonrk, on show, from 355. to £lOO, forming a dileitY so impressive that we are almost

STRUCK DUMB WITH AMAZEMENT. We now go up stairs to the Dining-room Showroom. wkat a sight, long avenues of Sideboards is the first impression ; hundreds of Sideboards, with hundreds of Suites, also Dining !Tables, Overmantels, splendid colleciion of Bronzes, Ormolu Clocks, Vases. THE Anglo-American crisis has The Anglo- gone through several phases American Crisis. since the now historical message of President CLEVELAND was cabled to the country in the middle of last week. At first there was a disposition to scout the mere possibility of a war between England and the United States. It was declared that such a disaster was impossible and even "unthinkable." But a closer scrutiny of the point at issue and particularly of the precise language used by President CLEVELAND did not, in the first instance at all events, tend to diminish the fears of a rupture. The consequence was , something in the nature of a panic on the stock exchanges. American securities went down with , a rush, and the losses sustained by Yankee inves- tors have been estimated at between fifty and two hundred milions of pounds, though prob- ably oven the smaller of these sums is an ex- aggeration. The next phase was a gradual return of public confidence. Influential voices on both sides of the Atlantic were raised in protest against the mere contemplation of a resort t 3 hostilities for the purpose of settling what is in itself an extremely small matter. It began to 4 be seen in the United States that a bound- ary dispute between a British colony and Venezuela might be settled. very easily without a violation of the Monroe doctrine. In England there was no dispositiou to talk or write dis- respectively about the said doctrine. It was even very generally admitted that the proposition which was first openly enunciated by President MONROE was, from the American point of view, an eminently reasonable one, and one which Great Britain would not be slack in upholding if she were placed in the same position as the United States. As a matter of fact, it has been pointed out that so far from this country being hostile to the Monroe doctrine, the first announcement of the doctrine as guiding rule in American diplomacy was encouraged if not actually sug- gested by the British statesman, CANNING. it is natural that Americans should be strongly op- posed to any further acquisition of territory on their continent by any one of the larger States of Europe. If, for instance, there was to be a scramble amongst European nations for South America just as there is at the present time for Africa the position of the United States would be altered very much for the worse. Instead of being ahle as now practically to confine its energies to the arts of peace, it would be placed under a neces- sity to increase both its army and its navy to meet, if need be, the aggressions of powerful neighbours. The force of these arguments are freely admitted in this country, but, it is just as freely asked,what relation have they to the Anglo-Venezulan dis- pute? The Venezuelans in addition to claiming a large extent of territory bordering upon British

Guiana, declare that they are entitled to slices of country which has been colonised by British sub- jects and administered by British officials for many years. The British . Government as a matter of course rejects this latter part of the claim, but as to all the rest of the territory in dispute it is pre- pared to accept the award of an arbitrator. There is clearly no violation of the Monroe doctrine as originally laid down in the position taken up by Great Britain, and there are now many indications that the people of the United States are beginning to look at the affair in this light. At the same time it would be premature to conclude that all causes of friction between the two +countries have been removed. A good deal will depend upon the report of the commis- sion which is to be appointed by the American Government to inquire into the merits of the dis- pute. If that commission recommends tha.; the whole of the Venezuelan claims should be sub- mitted to arbitration, the crisis may become more acute and threatening than ever. But on the other hand the delay caused by the inquiries of the commission will give ample opportunity for the development of the enormous forces which tell in favour of peace between the two communi- ties. In the States the jingo spirit which was aroused by the PRESIDENT'S Message was speedily rebuked by some powerful newspapers and by a number of eminent citizens. It is reported that on Sunday after Dr. LYMAN ABBOTT had preached a strong anti-war sermon in the Plymouth Church, Brooklyn, the vast congregation so tar departed from the usual decorum of a religious service as to burst into prolonged cheering. ' Another popular transatlantic preacher, the Rev. Plaiintrasr, strongly condemned war, and suggeSted that the United States should join Great Britain in rescuing the Armenians. And, on the whole, these two Ministers seem have voiced the sentiments of the Christian churches of America. On this side of the water some remarkable expressions of opinion have been evoked mainly by the enterpriso of the conductors of the New York "World," which was the first in- fluential American newspaper to criticise the Message of President CLEVELAND. The most no- table replies which the "World" has received to its inquiries are from Mr. GLADSTONE and from the PRINCE of WALES. Mr. GLADSTONE urges that "only common sense is required" to remove all possibility of disagreement; while the PRINCE of WALES earnestly trusts "and cannot but believe that the present crisis will be arranged in a manner satisfactory to both countries, and will be suc- ceeded by the same warm feeling of friendship which has existed between them for many years." This is a wish which will, it is to be hoped, be effectively endorsed on both sides of the Atlantic.
THE "perils of the sea" have been The Storm, sadly exemplified during the pre-

sent week on the East coasts of both England and Ireland. The scene in Dublin Bay on Tuesday was a particularly deplorable one. Early on the morning of that day a largo sailing ship was seen battling with the wind and waves. She made an attempt to reach Kingstown ha-:bour but was not successful, and then appeared to be drifting rapidly upon the rocks. Her sailors sent up signals of distress, and in response to these the life-boat was brought out and was raoidly manned with a crew of fifteen gallant watertnen. The sea was raging terrifically at the time and the boat was covered again and again by the irresistible waves, but still the crew persisted in pushing forward towards the distressed vessel. By desperate and unflagging efforts half the distance was cove red, when suddenly the lifeboat was seen to corn-

thrown into the water, and it is reported that not one of them has been saved. In spite of this disaster a second but smaller lifeboat was launched, and manned with another crew of fif- teen, several of whom volunteered for the danger- ous duty on the spot. This boat was also capsized, but fortunately it quickly righted itself and all the crew were able to clamber back to their places. On another part of the Irish coast, near Dungar- von, a still more tragic scene was witnessed on Tuesday. The Moresby, a large vessel from Liverpool, there went ashore and went to pieces. Amongst those on board were the Captain's wife and his little son. When the vessel finally broke up the captain strapped his child to his back and attempted to swim to the shore. It was a forlorn hope, and both father and son were overwhelmed by the waves. The cap- tain's wife was seen by the crew of a Dungarvan lifeboat struggling in the breakers and she too fell a victim to the storm. Out of the crew of this vessel no fewer than nineteen were drowned.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Tuesday afternoon, the fortnightly meeting of this Boatd was held in the Board-room at Dutton Workhouse. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Knowles, and in addi- tion to the members of the Rural District Council, there were present Mr. A. R. Norman, Mr. S. Yarwood.Mr. J. Ashton (c.lerk), and Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), and Mr. Cunnah (workhouse master).

div.head: PROPOSED SEVERANCE OF MORLEY.
div.p: THE PROPOSED SEVERANCE OF MORLEY.

The Local Government Board writing with reference to the proposal to transfer the township of Norley from the Runcorn Union to the Islurthwich Union. sent a copy of a letter addressed to the clerk of the Norley Parish Council saving the Board had given the matter their careful consideration. hut in view of all the circum- stances of the case they are of opinion that nu sufficient reason has been shown for altering the present constitu tinn of the Runcorn Union as proposed by the memorial late.

div.head: ADDITIONAL MALE WARD.
div.p: ADDITIONAL MALE WARD.

Mr. Eteywpod moved that the Board consent to the erection of an additional ward for males in accordance with a plan to which the Local Government Board had affixed their seal, at an expenditure of £lso,and that the amount in question be borrowed,to be repaid in 20 years. —Mr. T. Wright seconded themotion, and it was carried.

div.head: FIRST AID TO TIM INJURED.
div.p: FIRST AID TO TIM INJURED.

Mr. Yarwood mentioned a case in which Nurse Hughes had acted with great credit to herself. Some short time ago a man engaged on the new building accidently cu,. several of the tendons of his wrist, and made altogether a fearful gash. Nurse Hughes stopped the flow of blood, and bandaged the wound. After- wards the man was taken to Dr. Robinsm, of Runcorn, and that gentleman said he was sorry he had unwrapped the bandage, because a surgeon could not have better dressed the wound.

div.head: WESTON POINT.
div.p: WESTON POINT.

SCALDING ACCIDENT—On Friday morning, Richard Green, of Post Offir,,,road, Weston Point, met with serious injuries whilst following his employment at the Salt Union Works. He was standing on the end of a pan of brine, when his light went ont,and he slipped and fell in. Mth his legs up to the knees wereseverely scalded. He is under the medical attention of Dr. McKenzie.

In a discussion on the Navy Estimates in the French Senate on Tuesday M Lockroy said the French fleet was equal t 3 the combined navies of the triple Alliance. He did not wish to establish a comparison with Eogland,but he thought that in a few years France would possess a powerful maritime force.

div.head: 'ME EXAMINER SATURPAY, DECEMBER 28, 1895.
div.p: 'ME EXAMINER SATURPAY, DECEMBER 28, 1895.
RUNCORN TONIC SOLFA. PRIZE CHOIR.

THE "M ESSIAH." It was most appropriate thai the " Messiah ' should be selected as the piece to be rendered on the eve of Christmas by the Runcorn Tonic Solfa Prize Choir—a choir which has already won laurels in open competition and bids fair to become famous. If evidence were needed that the inhabitants of Runcorn are a musical people it was forthcoming on Monday night when perhaps one of the strongest choruses that ever appeared on a Runcorn plat- form discoursed music which was a credit, alike to the choir and the town. The leaQing artistes at the performance on Monday, when the Public gall was well filled, were Miss Bessie Holt (soprano)- Madame M. Fish (contralto), Mr. H. Berry (tenor), and Mr. T. B. Maude (bass), and they creditably per formed the parts allotted to them,although it must be ad- mitted that many a better quartette has appeared before a Runcorn audience. Miss Bessie Holt was perhaps the best of the four, her finest contribution being the diffi- cult air " Rejoice greatly," and that most beautiful and tranquillising air " I know that my Redeemer liveth." Mr. Maude effectively sang " Why do the nations so furiously rage together,"and the air" The trumpet shall sound "was highly popular with the audience but the palm of honour with regard to this must be awarded the trumpeter—Mr. Taylor of Liverpool, whose performance was masterly. The chief interest in the concert however lay with the chorus, consisting of fully one hundred local voices,and their performance was one that will not be soon forgotten. From their first chorus " And the Glory of the Lord "in all its sublime simplicity, to that inimitable final " Amen," their numerous pieces were given in a manner which fascinated the audience who were not slow to show their appreciation in unmeasured terms. A capital rendition was given of the powerful and effective chorus " For unto us a child is born " with its grand burst of voices and instruments on the words " Wonderful, Counsellor." One might go on describing the w. ole series of choruses which were all given with extraordinary brilliancy. The chorus " He trusted in God," in which the great spectacle of Christ being scoffed and jeered at by the crowd when on the cross is vividly represented ; the inspiriting piece " Lift up your heads," and that majestic and un- approachable "Hallelujah" all received a treat- ment which left nothing to be desired. Dur- ing the performance of the " Hallelujah chorus," the audience seemed to b 3 spell-bound, and at its close they gave vent to most intense applause. This chorus seems to have an overpowering effect,and one can well believe Handel, in speaking of the sensation he experienced in composing it, when he said, " I did think I did see all heaven open before ine,and the great God Himself." In the performance of the " Messiah" the instrumental orchestra pTays an important part. The oratorio is as- sociated with most beautiful and charming movements, and in many of the pieces sung, a dramatic effect is in- troduced by the orchestra. In addition to accompanying the vocalists, the tuneful overture and the charming pastoral symphony which is ever an attractive feature of the " Messiah,' were exceedingly well played by the instrumentalists, who although not numerous gave a finished performance. Mr. J. Holford, the hon. conduc- tor, is to be congratulated upon the way he has tutored the members of the choir, and brought it to such a state of efficiency. Mr. W. Cooke capably fulfilled the duties of organist.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
A RUNCORN TEACHERS' APPOINTMENT:

Miss Staveley, an assistant teacher at the Parish Church schools, has been appointed headmistress of a new school near Wigan. During her stay in Runcorn her services have given the greatest satisfaction. A MINISTER AND PEOPLE IN HARMONY.. _

The local Methodist Free Church circuit, consisting of two churches, one in Ellesmere-street Runcorn, and the other at West Bank, Widnes has during the week unani- mously invited the Rev. John Stafford to continue their pastor until August 1897. RAILWAY TONTINE CLUB, RUNCORN. • . .

The annual meeting was held at the Railway Hotel on Thursday evening week when the members received a dividend of 165. U. The statement of accmints was submitted by Mr. Darlington, treasurer. The officers appointed for the following year are—Mr. Davies, presi- dent; Mr. A. Sant, secretary ; Messrs. J. Lambert and J. Beckett, stewards. A preasant gathering was spent,and songs were contributeci by Messrs. Lambert,Le Couteur, Hinds, and Watson.

There passed away at her residence at Rhy I during Wednesday night at an advanced age, Mrs. Johnson, relict ef the late Mr. Thomas Johnson, who for some years resided at the Grange, Runcorn. The deceased lady had been a sufferer for some time. Her husband was a member of he firm of Messrs. John and Thomas Johnson, of the Runcorn Old Soapery. They were ex- ceedingly well-known and greatly respected in the town. They were intimately associated with Trinity Church, and the living was at their disposal.

div.head: .. INTERESTING PRESENTATION.
div.p: .. INTERESTING PRESENTATION.

On Sunday afternoon an interesting presentation took place in connection with St. Michael's Sunday school, when the teachers presented a family Bible to Mr. James Blundell, one of the teachers, who it may be stated was married at Widnes on Thursday :morning. The Rey. A. J. Jameson opened the proceedings with a few appro- priate words, alluding to Mr. Blundell's work in con- nection with the school and choir. Mr. Pownall, in making the presentation also referred to the services of Mr. Blundell, speaking of tlis willingness to help in Christian work. Mr. Blundell suitably responded and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: 'DEATH OF MR. BROOKFIELD.
div.p: 'DEATH OF MR. BROOKFIELD.

The death occurred on Tuesday of Mr. Brookfield, of IFairfield-road, Liverpool,at the age of 57 years. He was 1 well-known in Runcorn in-as-much as he had for a period of 30 years held the position of accountant at the Run- c,srn Soapery and Alkali Works, now in the hands of the United Alkali Company. It will be remembered that early in the present month Mr. Brookfield had a paralytic seizure in Lowland-road when proceeding from the train to the office. He was immediately attended by Dr. McDougall who ordered his removal home. Despite all attention he died as stated. IMPORTANT APPOINTMENT OF THE REV. F. C. SALARY!). The Rev. F. C. Salkeld, son of Mr. W. F. Salkeld, Heath-road, Runcorn, has been appointed to the rectory of Barcheston, Shepston-on-Stour, in the diocese of Wor- cester. On the 18th of the present month he was in- stituted by the Bishop of Worcester, and read himself in on Sunday last. It may be stated that the living is of the net value of £225 per annum with a chaplaincy of £52 a year, a rectory (once a monastery) and 14 acres of glebe in the gift of the Rev. 0. C. Wright. The church is one of the oldest in the diocese having been built in 1291, and completely restored in 1870. The new rector of Barcheston has spent a number of 3 ears in Ceylon and India, and bad to relinquish the post of chaplain of Asansol-with-Rancegan3, Bengal, on account of ill. health. DEVONSHIRE TONTINE SOCIETY, RUNCORN.

The annual supper in connection With this society was held at the Devonshire Hotel, on Thursday night week, when about 40 members sat down. It was pro- vided by Mr. A. llaining, and served up in first-class style. After the tables were cleared Mr. W. Sherratt was elected to the chair, and the Secretary read the ac- counts of the year, showing the receipts to be £lO9 53. 4d., and expenditure £6O 53., leaving a balance equal to 143. 91. per member. This was considered very satisfactory. The remainder of the evening was spent in singing, Sicc.. songs being contributed by Messrs. A. Claw, H. Evans' D. Elwards, W. Evans. H. Coleshill, E. Turner, and W. Harvey. A pleasant evening was spent.
FIRE IN A DWELLING-ROUSE.-NARROW ESCAPE OF
CHILDREN.

What might have bee-n—a—most serious matter indeed occurred in Vicar-st. on Christmas evening,at the house tenanted by Mr. William Fletcher. Messrs.B.Crosby and Cooke were returning from the choral service which had been held in St. Paul's Church, when they saw that the cufzains in one of the rooms at the house mentioned were on fire. They immediately entered the house, the front door .9f which was open, and found that the only occupants were three young children. The youngest, a child only a few months old, was lying under the win- 3W, and some of the pieces of the burning curtain had .allen upon the clothes which wrapped the child,and set them on fire. With all possible haste the fire was extin- guished,and this was accomplished before much damage bad been done. The child was fortunately very little burnt. The other children were from two to four years of age. It is a matter of course to say that but for the timely assistance of Messrs. Crosby and Cooke the child- ren might have been burnt to death. The grandmother of the children arrived on the scene after the fire had beeß put out. " THE PAY OF THE PIED PIPER."

There was -again a large audience in the Runcorn Public Hall,on Friday evening,when the children attend- ing Greenway-road Board Schools repeated their per- formance of the operetta with the above title. In addi- tion, a short miscellaneous programme had been arranged to fill the time occupied at the previous concert in the distribution of prizes. Mr. William Blackledge, of St. Helens,gave a number of his humerous sketches in his inimitable fashion,which greatly delighted the audi- ence. Mr. Blackledge is rapidly coming to the front as a first class humorist,and last week he was awarded first prize in a humorist contest at Crewe, in which most of the best talent in the country competed, for his per- formance of " Our Village Choir Concert." The other miscellaneous items included a nautical drill, " The Jolly Tars," in which a score of lads took part,under the conductorship of Master Williams ; action song, " The Milkmaids," by 20 girls ; action song," Ten Little China- men," by ten boys ; and a musical medley performed by 12 girls. The whole of the items were given in a most creditable manner,and reflected great credit upon the teachers. Miss Kilburn and Miss B. Hill accompanied. The receipts of the concerts are in excess of last year.

div.head: STOCKTOIsf HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTOIsf HEATH.

A axPPLETON PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE—This committee met at the London Bridge Inn, Stockton Heath, on Friday last week. Mr. Henry Eves occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. Davenport, J. Whit- ' low, Ashton Hares, Pearson, Hugh Darhyahire, Cop. pock, Marsh, and Mr. J. Ashton (clerk) ; Mr. Swinton (surveyor), and Mr. Farrington (nuisance inspector). A letter was read from Mr. Henry Hunter engineer of the Ship Canal Company with reference to a road at Stockton Heath, stating that it had been carefully examined and they found that the damage which had occurred to it was al- tegether due to a sewer which had been laid by the County Council (or other authority, he did not know which) which had no nutlet, and through which the sur- face of the road was blown up after any heavy rainfall. It would therefore be well for the authority to take the matter up with those who laid the sewer.—Mr. Stan- hope Bull, county surveyor, writing with reference to the road in question, said it WAR still under tho charge of the Manchester Ship Canal Company.—The Clerk reported that he had forwarded a copy of the last men- tioned letter to the Manchester Ship Canal Company but had received no reply:—Mr. Thonias Berry, estate agent of the Brideowater trustees wrote with respect to the lighting of streets at Stockton Quay. He understood, that the private streets on the Bridgewater Trustees' Estate were not liehted, and that some ohiection was raised by the authority to lighting them until they were completed. He pointed out that in every district with which the trustees were con- I cerned the nunlic authorities lighted the private streets before they were completed. He asked for the matter to be brought forward.—lt was resolved on the motion of Mr. Pearson, seconded by Mr. Whitlow. that 1 the ennsideralon of such letter and the question of , lighting streets be referred to the Lighting Committee.-1 A communication was read from the Town Clerk of Warrington, and the report of the Borough Surveyor therein referred to with reference to the disposal of the Wilderspool sewage. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Davenport, seconded by Mr. Pearson, that with the exception of the pipe sewer from tha manhole at the junction of Greenall's Avenue being a 15 inch Pipe instead of a 12 inch,the renert and scheme of the Borough Surveyor of Warrington be approved.—With reference to the suggested change of duties of surveyors of the Rural Council the committee were of the opinion that Mr. Swinton should continue to ant as surveyor of the highways and that he he apnointed inspector of Nuis. ances. and the Tnsnector under the Dairies, Cowsheds, and Milk Shops Order of 1885,and have assigned to him, the parishes Annletnn. Granpenhall, Latchford With- out, and Thelwall, and that Mr. Farrington he relieved of the duties of such offices in the parishes mentioned, and that Mr. Swinton he requested to reside in one of the Parishes —The committee also resolved that the Council he requested to draw the attention of the Manchester Shin (lanai Company to the &tiny rous state of Stag Bridge, Walton, Twenty Steps Bridge, ctockton Heath, and Knutsford-road bridge, and that they he requested to strew sand on the bridges in frosty weather to prevent slipping, and that it he commenced as early as six o'clock in the morning.—These minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Davenport. seconded by Mr. Knowles, at the meeting of fhe Rural Council on Tuesday.

div.head: DENSE FOR. DROWNING _CASES IN RU,VCORN AND DISTRICT
div.p: THE DENSE FOR. DROWNING _CASES IN RU,VCORN AND DISTRICT

The dense fog which prevailed at an earlyhot.ir-On Friday morning until the following day has been the cause of loss of life in Runcorn and district. The first Fatality reported was that at Preston Brook. It appears that early in the morning Joseph Johnson, Alfred Clare, Abraham Speed, Jonathan Holt, residing in the Preston Brook district, and Eiwardlllill, of Cawdor-st.,Runcorn, fell into the Bridgewater Canal, when going to their work. Four of them were saved, but Joseph Johnson was drowned. He and Clare were proceeding along the bank together when Johnson stumbled into the water, ' and his companion did the same a moment later. Clare succeeded in getting out, but with great courage re- entered the canal for the purpose of rescuing Johnson. In his plucky attempt he almost lost his life, and if it had not been for the timely appearance on the scene of William Webb, doubtless this wmuld have been the case. He was rescued in an exhausted condition. The body of Johnson was recovered an hour later. At the inquest on Friday afternoon, before Mr. J. E. Worslev, it was stated that deceased was 35 years of age. The above facts were given in evidence, after which a verdict of "Accidentally drowned " was recorded.—On Friday night, a young woman, 19 years of age, named Marzaret Pickering, School-lane, Weston Point, fell into the Ship Canal at Weston Point, and was also drowned. Another drowning case was also reported on Saturday morning. A night watchman at Highfield Tannery,named Thomas Chamberlain, on returning home at 5.30 a.m. on Satur- day fell into the Bridgewater Canal, and when rescued from the water life was extinct. At Hale Bank, near Widnes, nn Saturdav morning, the body of a man named Edwin Jones, 52 years of age, of Halewood, was found in a pit of water eight feet deep. It is surmized that he fell into the water on his way from work.—De- ceased laboured at Golding Davies' Chemical Works,Wid- nes. Many narrow escapes are also reported. On Friday morning William ITodgaon. of 6, Lord-street, who is en- gaged at the Runcorn Dlcks, had a most unpleasant ex- perience. He fell into the dry graving dock, a depth of 12 or 14 ft., but escaped without any further injury than a badly sprained ankle. John Booth of Canal-street, Runcorn, aged 18, when going to his work at Mr. Rey- nolds' Tannery, narrowly escaped being drowned. He fell into the Bridgewater Canal, byt fortunately his cries for assistance were heard by some boatmen employed by Mr. Jonathan Florsefield. John Tomlinson, by means.ni a bnathonk, rescued him when in an unconscious condi- tion. Efforts to restore animation proved successful. Mr. J. E. Worsley held two inwiests in the Police Office at Runcorn on Monday. The first taken was that on the body of Margaret Pickering.—Ann Pickering iden- . . .

tided the deceased as her daughter who was 19 years of age. She was in a delicate state of health. On the even- ing of the 20th inst. she went out, and witness did not see her alive again.—Mary Ann Thompson deposed that she and deceased went to see some friends on the flat Richard which was lying alongside the canal wall at Weston Point. The deck of the vessel was about nine feet from the top of the wall, and in order to get on, she jumps(' on the riggings. She left the deceased standing on the wall. After witness had got on the vessel, the deceased jumped to get on the rigging, but missed doing en and fell into the canal between the vessel and the wall. It was then about ten minutes past ten, and it was foggy and dark at the time. She was sober at the time ; they had only two glasses of beer each. The deceased never came to the top of the water again when she fell in.—William Spruce, Batman on the Richard, stated that he saw the deceased jump from the rigging, but in doing so she fell between the vessel and the wall. He thought she caught her head against the wall in fall- ing. The flat was about three feet from the wall. They at once set to work to grapple for her, but the body was not found until the following day.—P.C. Bancroft, stationed at Weston Point, denosed that he recovered the body from the Ship Canal at 1.40 on Sunday. There , was a scratch on the right cheek.which might have been I done by the grappling irons, and also a wound at the back of the head. A verdict of " Accidental Death " was returned. The second inquiry was telative to the death of Thomas Chamberlain, Halton Brook.—The de- ceased was identified by his daughter who stated that he left home at five o'clock on Friday night to go to his work at flighfield Tannery. He was then in his usual health. It was a very foggy night.—William Plant stated that shortly after five o'clock on Saturday morn- ing he went to his work to relieve the decened who had been on duty during the night. Witness told deceased to go home by the , bottom road owing to the fog to which deceased replied ' that he did not think it was so bad. Witness said to him that it would be safer, and then went into the works. S'iortly afterwards he heard a cry for "help, help." He went to the hank of the canal, and he saw William Barker. Abram Adamson, and George Hollins- worth there. They shouted to him " your watchman is in." The deceased again shouted for help, and stated "I am over this side, I 'am standing on the bottom." Witness could just see his head by means of a lantern at the opposite side of the canal. A long pole was stretched towards the deceased but he could not get hold of itond he heard him say that it was all over with him.— The Coroner: Couldn't anyone swim? Witness: I couldn't say; there were throe at the canal side when I got there. —Abram Adamson. labourer, Heath-road, stated that on Saturday morning he was on the canal bank when he heard a cry for help. He moon afterwards heard another " Do help me, do help me." He hastened in the direction of the voice. Mr. Barker also came upon the scene with a lantern, and they got along prop, but the deceased did not grasp it. Witness went to the other side of the canal, and eventually succeeded in getting the deceased tt, the side. He tried to restore the deceased, and let the water run out of his mouth. In answer to questions by I the Coroner, witness stated that he could not swim, and , did nr t know anything of pumping the water out of the man or the way to work his arms.—William Barker, 39, Stanley-street, a labourer also saw the deceased in the water. It was about 530 when he heard someone cry for help: He was working at the time, and put on his coat and took with him a lantern. He put the lantern on the top of his head, and was just able to see the deceased's face at the top of the water. They had to travel about a quarter of a mile to get round to the other side. He could not swim and did not know methods of restoration. The Coroner having characterised the case as a very sad one, a verdict of" Accidentally Drowned" was returned.

Two little boys of five wer; playing with matches nut side a jute warehouse at Dundee on Christmas D tv. Some loose jute caught fire, the flames; spread to the bales inside the warehouse, and the brigade could not extinguish them. The warehouse was destroyed, and damage to the extent of about £6,000 was done. The boys were arrested, but released on account of their age.

div.head: CHRISTMAS DAY IN RUNCORN.
div.p: CHRISTMAS DAY IN RUNCORN.

, Christmas Day in Runcorn was observed in the cus- tomary quiet manner. The weather was bleak and cold and was not favourable to outdoor enjoyment. Special services were held at the Roman Catholic Church, and the Established churches in the morning, and at night, there was a performance of selections from Handers " Messiah "in St. Paul's Wesleyan church. There were also several entertainments. In the afternoon 300 poor children were most generously entertained at a hospit- able board in St. Edward's Catholic School. A football match between Runcorn and Hull was to have taken place, but Hull decided to pay £2O into the Runcorn exchequer in preference to making the journey at this time of the year. The number who journeyed by rail from Runcorn WAS very small in consequence of the meazre railway arrangements—the trains running as on Sundays. Tha work at the Post Office was in excess of last year, both as regards despatches and receipts of otters, literature, and parcels. The full staff was en- gaged and got through the work in an expeditious man- ner. An early breakfast was provided the staff, the caterm being Mr. Riley, Church-street. HOT-POT DINNER FOR CHILDREN. There was a merry gathering in St. Edward's Catholic Scho3lB about two o'clock on Christmas Day, when over 300 poor children were regaled with a substantial hot not dinner which had been inaugurated by the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi. Provision had been made for over 400 chit- then but not more than 300 availed themselves of the dinner provided. The treat was organised with the assistance of the members of the League of the Cross and the children of Mary. The hot pot was of first class quality. The pstaton fcr it had been kindly given by Mr. Stokes. of Rock Savage ; and the ingredients for the excellent plum pudding were provided by Mrs. Nixon and Miss Dixon. At the close of the dinner each child was the recipient of an orange from Mr. Morris. There was a willing band of assistants to attend to the wants of the children, including Miss Nixon, Miss Dixon, Mrs. Nixon, Mrs. Herbert, • Mrs. Quinn, Mrs. Haley, Mrs. Caskey, Mrs. Fahy, Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Byrne, and other members of the congregation at St. Edwards. The Rev, Dr. Gastaldi who has taken a commendable part in pro- moting the dinner, which was given to children irrespec- tive of sect or creed, was unable to be present owing to indisposition, but he was represented by the Rev. John Donovan S.J. M.A., who welcomed the children and 1 , wished diem a very merry Christmas and a Happy New Year. He intimated that the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi had de- cided to make the event an annual one. The band of the League of the Cross played selections durin4 the dinner. The bright and happy faces of the children were proof of their pleasure at the kindness which was extended to them. As the number present fell short of what was anticipated, the remainder of the viands were distributed among the poor of the district during the morning. Amongst the liberal donors to the fund may be mentioned the name of Dr. Robinson.

div.head: PERFORMANCE OF THE MESSIAH AT
div.p: THE PERFORMANCE OF THE MESSIAH AT
ST. PAUL'S.

There was a very large gathering at St. Paul's Wes- leyan Church on the evening of Christmas Day at the Christmas festival under the auspices of the St. Paul's Men's Bible Class. The proceedings were commenced at 6.30 with a short organ recital by Mr. William Cooke. The selections given were as follows :—Fantasie and Fugue, G. Merkel ; soprano melody, H. Smart ; great prelude and Fugue in D., J. S. Bach ; Berceuse in D. G. Herman. A choral service was then proceeded with,and selections from the " Messiah " given. An augmented choir, consisting of about 70 voices and a dozen instru- mentalists as under the conductorship of Mr. B. Crosby. After the opening hymn" Hark the herald angels sing, the Rev. T. Brackenbury engaged in prayer. The instrumental selections included the overture to the " Messiah " ; the pastoral um- , phony ; and an intermezzo by Mascagni. The organist contributed an organ solo " Offertoire upon two Christmas themes" A. Guilmant), and as a concluding voluntary, Finale 2nd Sonata (Mendelssohn). The choruses were exceptionally well sung. In the solo and chorus, " 0 though that tellest,"Miss Simkin creditably sang the solo. Miss A. Taylor was also successful in her rendering of several recitatives. The Rev. W. George and the president of the class (Mr. Kniveton), delivered addresses. Mr. Kniveton spoke of the usefulness of the class end extended a hearty invitation to all men to join the Bible Class. AT DUTTON WORKHOUSE. A most enjoyable day was spent by the inmates of Dutton Workhouse on Christmas Day. Morning service was held at sine o'clock, when appropriate carols were ' nicely rendered by the Choir. The Matron (Mrs.Cunnah) presided at the organ. The decorations though light, were effective, and suitable mottoes and shields adorned the walls. After service the Matron distributed a number of presents which had been received, consist- ing of books, pictures, arc., and the men received to- bacco. Diener was served at 12.30 in the large dining hall of the workhouse, and consisted of the usual Christ- mas fare, roast beef, potatoes, and plum pudding ; milk for the children, and the choice of milk or beer for the older inmates. All seemed to thoroughly enjoy their dinner, and showed their appreciation for the kind and genial manner in which it had been prepared for them, by giving three hearty cheers to the master and matron. Supper was supplied at 5.30 consisting of bread and cheese, milk and tea, and the men had the choice of milk, tea, or beer. At 6.30, the hall which had been prepared for the occasion, and looked quite bright and pretty with the numerous garlands, mottoes, banners and ehinese lanterns, arid was filled with young and old, eager to listen to the vocal powers and musical abilities of several of the inmates. The old and well- known inmate, George Thompson, highly delighted all bv playing several well-known and popular airs on the violin and mouth organ. The boys and girls in turn gave numerous songs and recitations in good style. Mr. Allison greatly pleased the audience with a comic song. A most happy and delightful day was brought to a close by the raising of three cheers for the Guar- dians, the ladies and gentlemen who had kindly contri- buted to the day's enjoyment, and the singing of the " National Anthem." The numerous gifts to the inmates had been forwarded by the following : G. Robinson, Runcorn ; Mrs. Rogers, Newton; Religious Tract Society per favour of Mr. Ormerod, Frodsham ; Mr. Mclntyre, Budworth ; Mr. and Mrs. Wright. Halton: Mr. A. R. Norman, Runcorn ; Mrs. Whitley, Stretton.; Mrs. Mars- den, Sutton ; Mrs. J. R. Chadwick, Runcorn ; Miss Best, Aston : Miss Maud Wakefield, Little Leigh ; Admiral Jonea Parry.Thelwall ; and tobacco from the Guardians.

PRIMITIVE MEMIODISr TEA AND CONCERT. In connection with the Primitive Methodist Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour, a tea and con- cert was held in the schoolroom, Greenway-read, en Christmas Day. A go,l number at down to tea which was served at 4.30. At the subsequent proceedings, which were of a most interesting character, the Rev. T. Bramhall presided. The first part of the programme consisted of the performance of the cantata, entitled " Bundle of Sticks," which was nicely given by the scholars in Miss Wilson's and Miss Lunt's class. Miscellaneous items comprised the second part of the nrogramme as follows :—Song, " One of the Queen's Navee, " Mr. Shingler ; song, "Old Arm Chair," Mr. J. Stubbs ; recitation, "Old Billy's Rose," Miss L. Efitchen ; song, " Mar- guerita," Mr. Pilgrim ; duet, " Call to Arms," Messrs. Shingler and Parry ; piccolo solo, "Gloria." Mr.J.Mack ; recitation, "The Newsboy's Debt," Miss Davies ; song. " Holy City," Mr. Parry ; song," 0 ! rest in the Lord," Mr. Williams ; recitation, "Beautiful Snow," Miss• Miles ; duet (selected), Messrs. Davies and Wfthingtcn. Mr.W. Grounds fulfilled the duties of accompanist. There was a large attendance. ST. JOHN'S.

In connection with St. John's Presbyterian Church a tea and entertainment was given on Christmas evening by a number of gentlemen. There was a good attend- ance at rea,the arrangements for which had been carried out by the gentlemen. The subsequent proceedings wers of a rather novel character, the gentlemen who contri- buted the various items assuming the names of British and Foreign birds. Altogether a most enjoyable time was spent. TEA MEETING AT CAMDEN.

The annual gathering in connection with Mr. Parker's Bible Class at Camden Sunday School, was held on Christmas Day. About 120 persons sat down to the ex- cellent repast provided, and a most inseresting pro- gramme was afterwards gone through, consisting of songs, recitations and readings. Various games were afterwards engaged in until Qunnor was served.

div.head: ST. HELEN'S THEATRE ROYAL.
div.p: ST. HELEN'S THEATRE ROYAL.

A strong company has this week produced Dion Rou- cicault'a familiar well-known Irish drama of "The Shaughraun." at the Theatre Royal, S. Helens. The humourous features of the story, inoluding the " wake " scene, have intensely delighted the audiences, while the portrayal of the more serious side have aroused the sym- pathies of the onlookers. The leading characters have been represented as under :—Arte O'Neale, Miss Edith Lewis; dare Ffnlliott, Miss Alice Ravnor ; Mrs. O'Kelly. Miss Sophie Shenton ; Moya Dolan, Miss Louie Mansell; Captain Molineur, Mr. Charles Vane ; Robert Ffolliott, Mr. Arthur Raynor; Father Dolan, Mr. John S. Hayden; Corry Kinchela. Mr. Arthur Lyle; Har- vey Duff, Mr. prank O'Grady; and Conn, the Erhaughraun, Mr. James Hackett. In reference to an advertisement in another column it will be Seen that the drama of "The Streets of London," will be presented next week. This is its first production in St. Helens and good houses are expected for the New Year holidays. A feature of the play is a great fire incident in which real firemen will appear with real fire extin- guishing apparatus. There will be a special performance on the afternoon of New Year's Day.

div.p: MARRIAGE OF MISS A. STRINGER.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
- - --- - ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

Warrington broke-tile-in- On-o-to—n-y-ti-little on Saturday, and managed to draw at Rochdale with the Hornets of that town. They were immeasurably the superior of the Hornets in every respect, and it was only by failing to utilise their chances that Warrington failed to win by a large margia. It is a great pity that they did not win the match for it would have raised them considerably in the League table, as it was, they only remained as they were.

The spectators .7ere very rowdy at Rochdale, andltbe poor referee go it hot from them. If they coetinue to act in a similar manner, they will probably not have the chance to " boo " the referee for a short or long space of time. The ground was not in a very favour- able condition owing to its hardness, but it was decided that the game should count as a competition match.

The feature of the match was the way in which the Warrington forwards beat the Hornets. Forward is supposed to be one of Warrington's weak spots, and it is therefore satisfactory that on Saturday at any rate, they had the measure of their opponents completely. The halves also beat the Hornet's halves while at three- quarters, Warrington wer, very well balanced, and it is in this division that Warrington's score cams from Cross being successful in scoring his first try of the season. Heesom had not much to do, and consequently his display was overshadowed by that of Rigg who had plenty of work, and it was almost mainly through his work that Rochdal esecaped defeat.

The most sensational match on Saturday was that between Oldham and Wigan. Previous to that match, Wigan had not had a point scored against them by a Lancashire club, and they had themselves scored 21 points. On Saturday their unique record was com- pletely broken, for Oldham who were in fine form piled on a goal and five tries to nil, and the Wigan re- cord read 21 points for, and 20 points against, a very ordinary record indeed. Wigan must have a screw looosa somewhere of late, for they were beaten the previous Saturday at Halifax by nine points to nil, and on the previous Saturday to that by Hull, by three points to nil. They were never noted for their powers at scor- ing, but their defence was considered to be almost the best intancashire. This opinion has been rudely shaken, from an adverse balance of from 32 points in three matches reads rather queerly.

Widnes came out of their shell on Saturday With vengeance, and trounced Barley to the turn of 20 points to nil. This reads very peculiar when the fact is taken into consideration that the previous Saturday to that they themselves were beaten to exactly the same extent by fluddersfleld. The last mentioned club has been having a good time of it during the last three weeks, for they have won three matches in succession with a record of 28 points to three. As previous to that they had only won two matches the whole of the season, they have reason to shake hands with themselves.

Bradford, after their temporary falling away, were as strong as ever, on Saturday when they per- formed a feat they have never performed before in a League match, for they beat Brighouse Rangers by a goal and a try to a try. The two Bradford clubs, Brad- ford and Manningham are very strong this season, anl will not be far from the top when the final comes.

div.p: TAKING COLD.

A " Cold " is not necessarily the result of a high or kw temperature. A person may go from a hot bath directly into a cold one, or into snow even, and not take cold. He may remain out in the coldest atmosphere until chilled through, and still not take cold. On the contrary,he may take cold by pouring a couple of table- spoonfuls of water upon some parts of his dress, or by standing in a door, or before a stove, or by sitting near a window or other opening, where one part of the body is colder than another part. Let it be kept in mind that uniformity of temperature over the whole body is the great thing to be looked after. It is the unequal heat upon amerent parts of the body that produces Colds, by disturbing the uniform circulation of the blood, which in turn induces congestion of some part. Beep the feet always dry and warm, avoid draughts of air, keep the system braced up by plenty of sleep and good food, and by a powerful Tonic, and you will be proof against a Cold and its results. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
R.S.P.C.A. CASES.

William Plinston,W; Ai-kin:street, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court, yesterday, with working his horse while in an unfit condition on Decembet 9th. In- spector Ellison, R.S.P.C.A., said that he saw the defend- dant in Ilorsemarket-st, with the horse and cart which was laden with iron and broken glass. The horse was very lame, and witness stopped him and examined the horse. It was in a weak and emaciated condition. The defen, dant was very abusive but witness elicited from him that the horse had been to High Leigh. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed.—John Foster, Penketh, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state on December 13th.—P.C. Delahay said that he saw the de- fendant with a grey mare in Irlam-st. The mare was in poor condition and on being examined two wounds were found, one on the shoulder, and the other near the neck, which were raw, and matter was oozing out.—Coun- cillor Roberts said that as far as he was concerned be would press for heavier penalties in cases of this kind next year. In the present case the bench would not be severe, and a fine of ss. and costs would be imposed.
AN-EE-CONVICT SENT TO GAOL AT WARRIN6TON.

On Saturday morning, before Messrs. J. Falselough, S. Wright, at the Warrington Police Court, James Walsh, alias William Collier, from Leigh, was charged that he being a person convicted on indictment and suspected of getting his living by dishonest means and refusing to give a satisfactory account of himself, was found in possession of a shawl, not being able to give satisfactory account of same. The Chief Constable (Mr L. Talbot) informed the bench that the prisoner was re- manded on Wednesday on a charge of being found in possession of a woman's shawl. The police, however. failed to find an owner for the shawl. Walsh was an ex-convict and under police supervision, and had not complied with the regulations.—Detective S. Monaghan repeated his evidence as already reported.—Henry Stock- well,assistant to Mr. Greaves, pawnbroker, Church at., said the prisoner offered the shawl for pledge on Tuesday at their shop. Witness called his attention to the shawl being damp, when he made an excuse saying that it be- longed to his wife, with whom he had a tift—Mr. Tal- bot said that on December 12, 1889, prisoner was Sentenced at Manchester to five years' penal servitude and three years' police supervision for shop-breaking. Be was let out of prison on December 11, 1894. Since then he had only worked three months. On Apal 13, 1895, he was again apprehended and sent for six months, Walsh came out if gaol on October 2 last. Mr. Talbot said that there were a number of such characters as Walsh now passing between Manchester and Liverpool. —Walsh was sent to prison for one month's hard labour. DRASTIC PUNISHMENT OF A. STATION LOAFER. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday before a full bench of magistrates, John Baguley (17) 5 Glassismise-vard. Scotland-road Was charged with hav- ing on the 13th December unlawfully obstructed Win. wick-street by standing there and preventing persons from passing.—He pleaded guilty adding as an excuse that he was waiting for a man who owed him a id.— P.C. Bruen said on the date named at 7.10 in the evening he was in Winwick-street and saw the defendant imped- ing several passengers from the Central Station. He was a complete nuisance and was the leader of a gang that Infested that place. There had been a number of com- plaints recently about this uuisance and particularly about defendant.—The Chief Constable said that he him- self had seen defendant and others loitering about the station and on the same date as the present offence he was approaching the station when these youths noticed him and rushed off in such a disorderly manner as to knock down an old woman who was passing. If these youths were going to make a nuisance of themselves in loitering at the Station he was determined to make it an expensive amusement for them. In reply to a question from the bench as to whether defendant was looking for work, Mr. Talbot said he was engaged in avoiding it.— As this was not his first !appearanee at court, and as an example to others, the magistrates inflicted the maxi- mum penalty of 40s. and costs (t 2 lifs.) or in default one month's hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH. POLICE COURT. TRlDAY.—Before Councillor Roberta (chairman), and Dr

Gornall. Datnormorms.—For this offence, William Dodwell and Duncan M. Scott, 75, Bewsey-road were eaeh tined ss. inclui- lug costs. A VIOLENT WOMAN—Mary Burns, Lythgoes-lane, was Charged with doing wilful damage to the door, chair, and chest of drawers the property of Thomas Soleil. Tanners. lane. on December 14th. Mr. Arthur Browne, who represented thelplaintiff. said that his client was Dr. Peacocke's coachman. Defendant and her husband were separated, and Mr. Burns lodged at the house of the plaintiff. On the night in question defendant came to Vaintiff's house and asked Soleil if he knew her. He replied that he did not. She then said " Well, lam a lady." Solan shut the daor and locked It, but defendant burst it open. She rushed in and spoiled the furniture above mentioned, saying that she wanted to see her husband. Evidence la support of the case was given, and defendant then denied that she had done any of the damage she was charged with. She said that ter husband had sent for her, and as Bolan would not let her in, she went in uninvited. A scuffle ensued in trying to put her out, but no damage to the furniture was done.—The bench fined the defendant in the costs. Mounay.—Before Mr. F. Monks (In the chair), Aldermen Harrison and Wright, COMMillor Pierpoint. Mr. T.Birchall. Mr. J. W. Hayward and Mr. John Fairclough. A QUIET MAN WHEN SOBER.—Thomas Hitch, ironworker, 7. Howard-street, was charged with being drunk and disor- derly In Bank-street on Saturday afternoon —Alter the case bad been proved the Chief Constable remarked that he was informed that defendant was a very inoffensive man when sober. He had behaved well while In the .• loek-up."—A fine of 2s. 6d. including costs was imposed. YOUTHFUL GASIBLEES PUNISLIED.—Riohard Baxter, 101, Sharp-street, James Crook. 63, Watkin-street. and James Connor, 49. Watkin-street, all lads of 14, were. charged with having on the 15th December Diayed a game of cards called banker " for money, in Foster-street. All pleaded guilty. P.C. Berry proved catching the defendants in the act on Sunday the 15th inst. He seized the cards and money which he now produced.—The magistrates ordered the defendants to be detained at. the Police Station for 48 hours. TVESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Ciarnett (chairman) and Dr. T. Starkey Smith. div.head: TRUE STATEMENT.
div.p: A TRUE STATEMENT.

I am going to make a statement at the outset of this article that will seem extraordinary. Here it is : Very few babies are born healthy. I think that statistics would show that the majority of persons in the world are born with some weak tendency. It may be a pre- disposition to one thing or it may be another, but cer- tain it is that perfect types of health are extremely rare. This applies to any age of life, but we can trace many diseases of adults to a weak tendency that shows itself in babyhood or childhood. This tendency to weakness is receiving more attention to-day in the scientific world than ever before, and the more are men inclined to believe that the real cause is a lack of vitality. Just what vitality is, may be difficult for some to understand. In plain words it is the measure of force of life. That is, vitality determines how much effort the physical and mental forces are capable of. Children born of healthy parents are frequently weak, and unless their vitality is increased, they show certain weak ten- dencies, the particular phase of weakness depending upon the nature of the child. Ordinary food does not nourish these weak children. Sometimes they live on, shew in imperfect development and signs of Scrofula, Ann nia,or Consnmption, accord- log to their tendencies, and again some wasting disease develops in childhood. nut their affections all spring nine times in ten, from the one source—low vitality. Consumption, Aorernia, Scrofula, Rickets, Marasmus —all are traced to low vitality caused by poor nourish- ment. The body is unable to assimilate food, and a gradual decline of the vital force is inevitable unless stips are taken to increase vitality and bring it up to a normal standard.
Here is a case in point "32, Glasgow-street, Newinzton, September 19:h, 1855. " Messrs. SCOTT & BROWNE, Limited, " 47, Farrington-street, E.C.

" DEAR Sins,—l have a little boy four years old, who was a very weak baby, and, until we tried Scott's Emulsian, he suffered greatly from Weakness and Nervous Debility. He was thin and emaciated, and his food did not seem to do him much good. We tried various tonics, but these also were of no avail. We began using Scott's Emulsion in June last, and you ought to see the change n the child. He picked up on Scott's Emulsion from the start. We gave him a teaspoonful after every meal, and it did him so much good that he now has a good appetite, has gained is flesh his nervousness has dis- appeared and he is,better in every ray.
_ " We can testify that Scott's Emulsion is the one remedy which gave our boy the nourishment his system craved.
" I feel sure that when once mothers have used Scott's Emulson to ,vercome the weak tendencies of their chil- dren, they will use no other remedy.
' Yours. very truly, Mrs. A.-LINDRIDGE."

The point I would emphasise in be foregoing letter is that Mrs. Lindridge's little boy was unable to assimilate his ordinary food. Of course, he grew thin, his nervous system became impaired, and his weak tendencies had their way. There are thousands ot babies, and adults too, who are not nourished by their food. Scott's Emulsion is just as beneficial to a person of fifty or seventy as it is to a baby. (1).

div.head: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION. WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE HORNETS.
div.p: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION. WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE HORNETS.

The Warrington first team journeyed to Rochdale on Saturday afternoon to meet the Hornets in their first fixture for this season. The weather was of a most Un- favourable character. There was a thick fog at War- rington, but as the team had received no communica- Moe from Rochdale as to the match being cancelled they proceeded on their jsurney by the five-to-one train to Manchester. The city was reached in good time. It had been arranged to proceed from Victoria Station tct Rochdale by a train which was timed to leave at 1.35, but on arrival at Victoria it was found that the 12 55 to Rochdale had only just gone, and the railway officials said the 1.35 would probably be an hour late. The fog also continued to be very dense, and with the prospect of being late in arriving at Rochdale it looked as though the match would have to be post- poned. About twenty-five minutes past two, the train left Victoria and proceeded at a very slow pace to Rectidale,which place was reached at three o'clock. Tne team at once proceeded to the Hornets' field, their arrival being greeted with cheers by a large crowd that had assembled. An inspection of the ground showed that it was utterly unfit to play upon. There had been a much keener frost in Rochdale during the previous night than thPre had beeu in Warrington, with the result that the ground, which is practically devoid of grass, was frozen quite hard. The Warring ten cap- tain at first declined to pier, the referee also agreeing that the ground was unfit for play. The spectators, to .the number of about 4,000. Ii id in the meantime been admitted to the ground, and it was therefore ultimately decided to play. The game, however, while counting as a League match, was really only an exhibition game. The play, however, was of an excellent character,and at times created great enthusiasm amongst the spectators. Almost from start to finish, Warrington had the best of the play,and were really the best team on the field. Had the match been properly contested, the visitors would have been the winners. Three of the Warrington team failed to appear, namely, Broady, Burton and Nevins, their places being taken by Carey, Foster, and Willcock. The Hornets had only one absentee. The teams were as follows : Warrington : Hee- som, full back ; Barber (captain), Cross, Carey, and Foster three-quarters ; Houghton• and Clarke, half- backs; Bsirrows, Fairhurst, Willcock, Harrett, Swift, Andrews, Taylor and Thornton, forwards. Rochdale Etornets,Rigg,full back ;IVightman,iridgeley,ll.Fletcher and Rangley, threequarters ; • Sutcliffe and Ramon, half backs; fliggin, Trevor, Whitley. A. Leech.flill, Dearden, P. Lech, and J. Fletcher, ferwards. The Hornets kicked off, but Warrington at once carried the ball inside the Rochdale quarter. Clarke went away with a run, and rot over the goal line, but failed to ground the ball. Rigg brought relief for the Hornets twice with splendid kicks In touch. At length the Warrington backs got posses- sion, and Cross, dodging well, gained a try in a good position. Heesom failing at goal. The Hornets played much better after this, and Warrington were compelled to touch down twice. •The Hernets also had a good op- portunity to score, but Midgley passed into touch. The homesters continued to attack very vigorously isp to the interval but there was no turther scoring. On restarting the visitors pressed. Midgley hroueht relief with a capi- tal kick, and Wightman was prominect with a run, but the visitors returned to the attack. Rig?, saved splendidly and then the Hornets took up the attack. Fletcher was given a pass by Raegeley, but he was tackled near the goal line. From the next scrimmage, however, Peter Leach scrambled over near one of the posts. S. Flanson's place kick sent the ball under the crossbar. The Hornets again took up the attack,hut five minutes from time the referee stopped the game on account of darkness. The result was thus a drawn game, each team having scored a try. Warrington played with good combination, the backs working nicely together,while the forwards gener- ally got the best of the opposing forwards. The match was a very pleasant one, and the home spectators ap- peared greatly pleased with the play of the visitors.

div.head: WIDNES v. BATLEY.
div.p: WIDNES v. BATLEY.

Played at Widnes before nearly 2.000 spectators on Saturday afternoon. A fog enveloped the ground. Both teams were strongly represented, and at three o'..lr;ck Barb-r started for Widnes. Goodall returned, hut Drummond sent the ball up the field, and Peters missed a good opportunity by failing La take Barber's pass. Brennan was called upon, but Batley were soon forced back on the defensive,Rispan and Peters distinguishing, themselves by smart tactics. Play was kept well with- in the visitors' 25, and Drummond was held inside the line, and a minute later one of the forwards dropped over, but the whistle called him back. Garner eventu- ally transferred to midfield, and after Brennan had kicked clear, Emery, Johnson, and Whelan led a fine forward rush, Garner being lucky in clearing. A free kick to Widnes availed them little, but an excellent punt by Nevitt put Widnes on the aggressive again. Garner sent them to the right about, and a touchdown was forced by Batley ; but after this a magnificent piece of play between Drummond, Barber Nevitt, and Rispan, and a good kick by Nevi t, ended in Arthur Peters scoring a capital try near the posts, and he after- wards kicked a goal from the place. Batley did some attacking after this reverse, but were held well in check by the home hacks, whom the hard state of the groluid suited. They made a capital run down the field, and upon this oerasipn H. Peters scored. Barber made a fine but unsuccessful attempt at goal, and the interval was called immediately afterwards. Half time :—Wid- nes, one goal, one try ; Batley, nil. In the second half the home contingent kept up the pressure, with the re- sult that at the close the score stood—Widnes, two goals one dropped goal, and two tries (20 points) ; Batley, nil.

HALIFAX V. 131714CORN.—Chl Saturday afternoon at Halifax, before 6.000 spectators. Wilson started for Halifax, and Firth soon made a grand run, but was pulled down by the visitors' full back. Capital passing, be Arnold and Rigg enabled Firth to run bekind, and he A ISO kicked a goal. Beautiful passing, in which all the Runcorn hacks tank part, resulted in the Halifax end being invaded, hut the pres:ure was relieved. Again the visiting backs did grand work, Warder only being held near the line. The game was remarkably fast, the Halifax hacks new shining in a line passing bout. The home forwards got off with a capital dribble, but Butter- worth neutralised it with a fine kick. Firth, who was playing brilliantly, ran to the Runcorn quarter, and kicked over Butterworth'a head, but could not recover the ball, and Runcorn cleared to the centre. Winskill made a grand run and scored, Firth failing. Flalf-time : Halifax, one goal one try ; Runcorn, nothing. Rigg, inaugurated the second half of the game by running in brilliantly from near the centre. Firth kicking another I goal. Runcorn then attacked strongly, and after fine I passing by their hacks Warder dropped at goal, just missing. The visitors were now having the best of tne I game, which continued wonderfully fast, the hacks on both sides treating the spectators to some splendid work. Runcorn for a while pressed severely, and were repeat- edly near scoring, but Halifax defended strenuouslY. Toothill made a run three-parts the length of the field, but Butterworth brought him down, and the visitcra by clever work, carried the loather back to the home line. In the last moment Robinson got a try for Runcorn, and Myers placed a goal. Result :—Halifax, 2 goals, 1 try (13 points) ; Runcorn, 1 goal (5 points). The game was a brilliant example of the Rugby game as it can and ought toile played. The forwards on both sides were wonderfully dashing—though here Halifax certainly had the pull—and probably there was some truth in the contention of their friends that the visitors were feeling the efferts of the long railway journey. The scrimmages were of the briefest, and almost invariably ended in a round of passing by the backs or a bit of dashing forward play. The back play of both sides was simply superb, and there was as much passing and running in this one game as is seen in half a-dozen aver- age matches. In theircombined work both seta were equally excellent, but the splendid individual efforts of Rigg and Firth deservedly secured Halifax the victory. Both sides had some hard lines, but these were equally shared. There was not a faulty player in the lot. Indeed, each man seemed to be at the very top of his form.

WARRINGTON " A" v. RneIIDALM TIORNETS " A."— These teams played their initial game of the season at Wilderspnol on Saturday, before a fair gate. Owing to the recent frosts the ground was very hard and being covered with a coating of frost presented a most wintry appearance. Warrington were not fully represented. The opening stages were confined to the Warrington quarters and Collier narrowly missed scoring in the first five minutes. Lawlass and Thomas cleared and a good dr)bbie was the means of play resting at half-way. A good passing movement by the hosne three quarters was spoiled by Buckley failing to take a pass, and the Hornets rushed the leather back to the home lines where IVhitworth had an ineffectual drop at goal. Spruce was compelled to concede a minor. From the kickoff, the Warrington front rank getting in nice working order, play was taken to the Hornets 25. mason secured and passing to Melledew and the player found neutral ground with a good kick. The Hornets' vangnard came along with a rush which was nicely stayed by Snruce who returned to half way. O'Brien, Bailey, and Lawless, took the hall to the Hornets' lines, and from a scrimmage Foden cleverly sclred. Lawless failed at god. On the restart Lawless made a coed run, and passing to Savage the latter scored an unimproved try, and half time arrived with the 'score, Warrington, 2 tries ; Rochdale, nil. Oa resuming, the Hornets pressed but coal not penetrate the defence. O'Brien and Foden were the means of the homesters attacking the visitors citadel, but Tweedale temporarily cleared ' the danger. Foden secured from a scrimmage and pass- ing to O'Brien he snored in a favourable position, but the kick was a failure. Final result, Warrington, 3 tries ; Rochdale Hornets, nil. The following were the

tams : Warrington : Full back,:Spruce ; threequarters, Bailey, Lawless, Thompson, and Buckley ; halt backs, Foden and O'Brien ; forwards, Savage, Hoyle, Hughes, E. Bailey, Savage, Scholtz, Monk and Litherland. Roch- dale Hornets : Full back, F. Tweedale ; threequarters, J. LATCHFORD RANGERS.— This match was played on the ground of the former. Both sides suffered through absenters. Latchford won the toss, the Saints' kicking off against the wind. The visitors pressed the home •team at the start, but some fine passing by the Saints' backs relieved, and from a scrimmage at half way Gregory got nicely away and passed to Caldwell who scared. Warburton and Bennett also scored tries, the Saints' leading by three tries to nil at half-tim,. In the second half the Saints' pressed con' tinually, Latchford b. int; bea:en at all points of the game, tries being scored by Warburton (one), Edgar (one), Hig,ginhottom (two), and Houghley (one). War- burton and Siddle placed the goals. Final St. Mary's two goals. six tries (38 points) ; Latchford Rangers, nil. WARE/NGTON ST. MARY'S V. RUNCORN.—TheSP teams met on Christmas Dr,y on the, Warringtoa Football ground, Wilderspool, before it lair attendance of specta- tors. A strong wind blew from goal to goal. Runcorn who were playing with the wind, pressed the St. Mary's severely, and Rmhardson scored shortly after the start. Higgintrottom passed to Mason, who ran nicely to half way, but this advantage was lost by a wild pass which enabled Runcorn to once more test Roughley, who was not found wanting, and play rested at the St. Marc's 25. Hampson was collared before he c•o)iii get in -hie stride, but the St, Mary's forwards took the ball to the Runcorn quarters. Warburton missed a pass, and Run- corn came on with a rush, but only a minor resultod. Runcorn still maintained the pressure, and Jolley just missed placing a goal from a free kick. Half-time : Runcorn 1 try, St. Mary's nil. On changing ends, St. Mary's played vigorously, and kept Runcorn on the de- fensive, but good opportunities were lost by wild pass- ing. Hig.ginbottom was almost a scorer, but a pass for- ward spoiled the chance. From now to the finish St. , Mary's penned their opponents on their lines, but owing to uncombined efbrts failed to penetrate the defence of the Runcorn backs.
