div.head: CHRISTMAS VACCINATION.
div.p: A CHRISTMAS VACCINATION.

"Crippled children are to be found in many towns outside London, and many a cripple might have been healthy, strong, and able to enjoy his Christmas plum pudding and playthings during Christmas time were it not for vaccination. A well known London surgeon once refused to remove enlarged tonsils from a boy ten ' years until the approaching Christmas had pas- sed, because he felt it would be so hard on the little chap to be unable to eat the good things that others would be enjoying on Christmas Day." My nearest, neighbour is a doctor, and as I was leaving my door I yesterday morning he was entering his. He said "Good 1 morning," and then made the above statement, after which he continued, I have just seen a case which 11 makes ma sad. A sweet little girl of eleven was vae.ci- nated the second time twelve days ago by a neighbour- ing doctor, a very competent man ; he chose the outer I side of the right leg, midway between the knee and the hip. In seven days soreness and redness were so marked and the fever so high, and the sore itself so deep and nasty and foul, that the parents became alarmed. The doctor used all his remedies that were likely to be of value to check the inflammation and lessen the fever. On the ninth day she was so bad that I was called in consultation. After we had thoroughly I examined the child we went into an inner room to talk the case over. As the doctor closed the door he turned quickly and said to me, 'Why does not some one discover a cure for the disease of vaccination ? " " Of.course you told him of V.V.V.?' I said. " Yes," he answered, " I did, and assured him that it was not only a cure but a preventative. At first he objected to giving what he called a patent medicine, but. afrer admitting that the child was growing worse, and the wound more foul, in spite of all his remedies, he agreed on my urgent recommendation to give it a trial. As usual, he had it transferred to one of hie own medi- cine bottles, and commenced giving it at once. That was three days ago. Within thirty-six hours the sore had lost its foul appearance,and had ceased to enlarge or grow deeper, showing clearly that, the antiseptic action of the medicine working through the blood had kitled , the germs that were producing this foul condition. To- day she is so well that I 'shall not be required again. I am rarely enthusiastic,but I must say that Vaccination Virus Vanquisher does its work no well that it will arouse enthusiasm in anyone." "If your child is doing so well, why do you speak of her as a cripple ?" I asked. " Because," he replied. " although the sore is now heal- ing, she will not be able to walk for at least ten days, and feels very keenly over her inability to go to the Christmas tree." The doctor stated further that he was convinced that if V.V.V. had been taken from two or three:days before vaccination was performed, and con- tinued regularly to the present,there would have been no cripple at Christmas time in that house. Judging by my experience in my own family I fully agreed with him.—The Weekly Record. To be had of all Chemists at 2s. 9. per bottle,or from the V.V.V. Company, Limited, 31, Snow Hill, E.C.,frem whom all who desire may obtain a descriptive pamphlet free of charge.

div.head: WARRINGTON FLORAL AND HORTI CULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON FLORAL AND HORTI CULTURAL SOCIETY.
ANNU&L MEETING.

The annual meeting of the above society was held on Monday evening in the lecture room of the Museum,Mr. Frank Grimshew occupying the chair. The treasurer's report was read by Mr. J. Fulton Smith. and he stated that the year commenced with a balance in hand of Ell 15s. 10d. This year, after holding two successful show.. they had succeeded in raising the balance to £l2 19s. 2d. Mr. Ryan, in giving the secretay's report, said that the committee sincerely thanked those ladies and gentlemen who had so liberally supported the society, and thus enabled it to carry on for the past two years. The summer show during the past year was held in the Gymnasium on August 20th to 23rd and was a distinct improvement upon the previous year, there being a large increase of exhibits. The crysanthemum show in Novemhertsvas also a decided emcees from a spectacular point of view, and the eommittee wished to thank Mr. John Crostield for so kindly supplying the large number of bulbs, and for offeting prizes. A satisfactory balance wag left at the end of the year, hut in view of the loss of time and incidental expenses of the secretary and treasurer, the eommittee had allowed them £5 each. —Councillor Smethurst in moving the adoption of the reports, said that he WAR sure that it WAR a very entour- aging report for a society which had started in such a humble war. He wished some of the gentlemen in the district about would follow the example of Mr. John Crosfield who had been so generous with his bulbs, and his offer ef prizea. He wished he could get the sympathy and the support of those other gentlemen,and get them to recognise the worth of the societv.—Mr. Lockhart seconded the motion which was carried un- animously.

Browne applied on behalf of Mr. Ihnmas Tunstall. of the firm of Messrs. T. and J L. Tunstall, for a music and dancing license for the late circus in Qleen-st. The building, he said, had undergone considerable alterations, a stage having been erected and other alteratinnq made, he thought to the satisfaction of of the Chief Constable, and he therefore applied for a twelve months' license for music and dancing there.

div.p: N EW B 50KS, NAG-AZINES, ETC.

eASSW:L AND CO.--Though only in its fourth year " Chums," as a boy's paper, has taken up an unapproachable position in the ranks of magazines of a professedly similar nature. Not only does it lead the way in literary value but the mandate of an enormous popularity among boys all over the kingdom has long since gone forth, with the result above mentioned. The volume for 1895 has just been issued and forms the best boy's Christmas pres- ent we can imagine, in that it provides attractions innumerable and lasting. Collectively the contents are :-12 coloured and tinted plates; over 1,000 pic- tures ; exciting serial stories (fully illustrated) by Robert Louis Stevenson, George Manville Fenn, D. H. Parry, Henry Frith, Andrew Home, and A. J. Daniels ; over 200 complete Stories ; over 130 chatty articles on subjects of special interest to boys; over fifty portraits of living celebrities ; over 2,500 anec- dotes, jokes, jottings,paragraphs about famous men &c. 'lnc serials are exceptionally excellent and possess all the attributes of the ideal conjured up in the minds of all lovers of the adventurous. Mon- archs of the Sea—a series of articles on some of our great ships, appeals directly to an Englishman's pride in his country's maritime supremacy and is also an exceedingly pleasant method I of instruction. No further attempt at detail is possible for the remaining contents of this large volume are too varied and equal in merit for individual mention. Not only is the reading matter unrivalled but the illustrations to it are very strik- ing and convey to the mind a correct view of the scenes and incidents so graphically described. No change has been made in the appearance of the volume, the lines of last year's model having been rigidly adhered to.—At the present season of the year when everybody is expected to be merry and joyful nothing comes more welcome than the new " World of Wit and Humour." Here we have en- tertainment and hilarity sufficient for a decade of seasons. Selections and stories by all the most humorous writers of the century are put up in a handsome green cloth cover with gilt lettering, and it is not rssh to state that a book-back seldom covered 480 more amusing and sidesplitting pages. No mater what a person's humour may be— whether sad or angry—tile cheering influence of " Wit and Humour " asserts its supremacy. The wild flights of literature here in print would move to laughter even a never-smiling Puritan of years ago could he be so fortunate as to get a glimpse within. This illustrator has also lent his art to the enhancement of the book and furnishes pictures almost as provocative of mirth as the lines surrounding them.—" Cassell's Family Magazine" has a special feature for the coming January nnmber in a complete story by Max Pemberton, written in that author's best style, and entitled " The Sword and Three," a relation by Nicolo Ferrara, the famous swordmaker, of an exciting occurrence happening to him in the latter years of his life but certainly, as the story shows, when his sword-arm had lost little of its "Quiver" for the first month of the new year, in addition to the general reading will contain a pictorial supplement, " Labours of Love for Christ's Lambs.

GEORGE NEWNES AND COMPANY.—Owing to the preqere, unsettled state of European politics and the seeming possibility of war in more directions than one, a new magazine from the offices of the above firm devoted to our naval and military strength and its human ana mechanical upholders, attracts special attention. Under the title of the "Navy and Army" we have presented to us a num- ber of beautiful photographs with explanatory text. No. 1 contains the reproduced photographs of Captain H RAI. the Duke of York, R.N., &c., Vice-admiral Lord Kerr, officers of the "Royal Sovereign," our heaviest battleship, and also a number of views on board the vessel itself. Rear- admiral W. R. Kennedy contributes a capable article on sport in the navy and declares in favour of that means of recreation for both officers and men. The army photographs include H.R.H. the Duke of Cambridge, Viscount Wolseley, noted regimental officers, a review of the Scots Greys, and an illus- tration of field artillery with a 12-pounder. Lieut- Colonel L. F. turner contributes an intoresting ac- count of recruiting work. All the illustrations are remarkably clear and well-defined and do credit to ticth printer and the original photographer. "The Navy and Army" is to be issued fortnightly and the price per number is 6d.—The " Sportfolio" and "Round London" still provide us good pictorial food, and have reached their 4th and 6th numbers respectivAly.—A new penny weekly magazine for ladieS—" Woman's Life" will be issued to-day (Saturday), and judging' from the early copy of the firs': number we have received it will meet with a warm reception. It will deal with every subject likely to interest lady readers, and the contribu- tions to its pages will be by the most up-to-date writers and popular artists. Fashions, stories, articles on all subjects, sketches, interviews, notes on home matters, &c., are all to be included. The pages are similar in size to those of the "Strand" and well printed. MACMILLAN AND CO.—We have again to announce , the arrival of books representing the Kingsley Pocket Edition, Illustrated Standard Novels, and The Tennyson People's Edition. Of the former "The Water Babies,s that engaging fairy tale for a land-baby, appears this week. The story is too famous to need more than a brief mention, and it suffices to say that it makes as neat and handy a , book as the rest of the series.—Benjamin Disraeli's " Sybil " is the last I.S.N at present before the public, and the introduction to the work is by Mr. H. D. Traill, who thinks with many others that if I the individual popularity of Disraeli's novels were ascertained it would come in a winner. He says " Those who read a novel frankly 'for the story' and want to be interested in plot and action rather than dazzled by dialogue, will certainly find in it more of what they seek than they will in any other of the Disraelian series." The other 14 pages of Mr. Traill's introduction prove conclusively his ability to tackle the subject of " Sybil " and the other works, and make interesting reading. Fred Pegrain's illustrations to the book are among the best we have seen —Two more of the chaste Penny- sonian Series are "The Princess" and "Will Water- proof," the latter including some 16 other short poems,. T. FreuEn UNwrtst.—We have to hand the 2nd annual eaition of the odd-looking little brochure entitled "Good reading about many books mostly , by their authors." As we explained beforo,this work contains a sort of review of well-known books,with reasons for their production, the formation of char- acters and scenes etc., by their authors in the majority of cases, or else by a competent authority. In all instances a photograph of the writer is given and altogether an unusually interesting series of papers is presented. A kind of fascination,amusing to reflect over, seems to attach itself to an author's. view of his own handiwork.—The price of the edition is is.

div.head: CAIRO•STREET CHAPEL.
div.p: CAIRO•STREET CHAPEL.

There was a good congregation at the Cairo-street Chapel on Sunday evening, when the Rev. W. H. Drum- mond, WA., preached a sermon upon the subject "What I believe ahout hell." The rev, gentleman combated the doctrine of an eternal material hell, and indicated what he believed to be the principal causes of the change in attitude of the majority of orthodox preachers in regard to this doctrine. _ _ _

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

On Sunday evenine selections from "The Messiah " were given in the above church by the choir, assisted by Mr. nirtin Schneider, who presided at the organ ; Miss Annie Nelson, soprano, and Mr. George Green, of the Cathedral Choir, all of Liverpool. There was a very large Congregation. and the collection, which was in aid of the organ fund, amounted to over £ll. Miss Nelson's items were " Rejoice greatly " and " I know that my Redeemer liveth " which she accomplished in a very able manner. Mr. Green, though suffering from A slight indisposition, sari; the te•ior music with great care, while with regasd to Mr. D. Fanshaw, Mr. J. H. Sherlock (bass), and Mr. F. Scattergood (alto), they net only did themselves su4tioe, but their excellent singing reflects considerable credit on St. Paul's choir, of which they are useful members. Mr. Fartshaw's beat Efferts were in " Thus said' the Lord " and " Who may ahide." Mr. S,!attergond did, well in the air "He was despised " and Mr. SherloA in " The people that walked in darkness." The choruses were remarkably well sung, and the whole performance was eminently satisfactory. Mr. J. J. Lythgoe, organist of St. Paul's Church, Ably conducted. BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHURCH.

On Sunday afternoon a choral service was held at the above place of worship presided over by the Rev. 0. Watkins, superintentent of the circuit. A number Chri‘tmas carols woe sung, and selections given by an efficient orchestral band of 18 performers under the able direction of Mr. F. Pendleburv, Mr. B. Wadsworth presiding at the organ. Some excellent vocal music was contributed by Miss Kent and Mr. Baker, and the band also played remarkably well, one of the items being Mr. Alfred It. Sutton's " Mendelssohn March." The pro- ceedings throughout were of a most enjoyable char- acter. A collection was made at the close of the service on behalf of the church funds, a satigfactory sum being realized.

div.head: AlAfrE'A'S 70 TiVAVZ/E2-117.
div.p: AlAfrE'A'S 70 TiVAVZ/E2-117.
A LOCAL HERO.

" Tit-Bits " for December 214 (of which we have re- ceived an advanced copy) contains the stories, jokes, poems, ke., which have won the numerous five-guinea grizes offered a few weeks ago. Spa jut interest is at- tached to one of them by Warringlou rrlere, inasmuch as it is contributed by Mr. H flardy.l9, Napler-streft, Warrington,and that one is"Flovv I won my medals." Mr. Hardy relates in a graphic manner exciting incidents which he witnessed or took part in in the Russian War, particularly at Balaclava and Inkerman. OF the latter, known among the s,.ddiers as " Bloody Inkerman," he says :—" I sounded boot and saddle at five a.m., at six we paraded (no breakfast ; we did Inkerman on an empty chest), before eight we had joined our division and were in position,ready to begin the havoc of that awful day. Shortly afterwards one of our guns was sent to occupy a point between two small knolls, on slightly rising ground, just sufficient cover for our gun- ners. I was sent with it ; 'during the first few rounds the result of our fire was visible, and I eaw lanes cut through the enemy as wide as a main street ; we soon had five men out of nine disabled. The officer in charge fell with broken wrist and a wound in the neck, from which the blood ran in a stream. We were about to limber up and join the emin portion of our battery, when our lieutenant gave a shout that went to our very marrow ; a gunner and myself had barely time to half drag,half cam our officer and place him between the trail and wheels when a detachment of Russians, about twelve or fifteen, were close upon us. They fired no shot, for they had none, as we found out afterwards, but meant to bayonet us and get the gun. We meant differently—our gunners (all big fellows) made rare use of hand-spikes and sponge staves. I saw three Russians braineid with the former ;
r§otber gunnar- amashed

the sponge in two for convenience, and" went for 'em." I had lost my sword earlier in the day, the upper sling had been shot away, it went without mv knowing it. In getting cur efficer's sword out of its scabbard I noticed his revolver, a seven-shooter; you may be sure I knew what to do with it. I was told after the brush was over that I didn't throw away a single shot, and if I tell the truth I think every man-jack of thoee grey-coats had eaten his last dinner. That was about the busiest five minutes I ever spent. Only two others beside myself and officer rejoined our battery ; of the rest, four had been killed, one mortally and two seriously wounded—hut we didn't lose our gun. Later on I was at my post when a ricochet shot took me at the back of my right leg, passed through my horse, and broke my left thigh. My mare fell on my leg, so preventing my getting away. I lay there a full hour, without even the relief of losing my senses. Twice cavalry passed over me, friends or foes I couldn't tell— I dared not move a finger even, le,t I should invite a Cossack lance. I was picked up with other odds and ends, and eventually sent down to Scutari, for I was a bad case. Youth anti a rare good constitution stood to me; in fourteen weeks I was at duty again, as cheeky as ever, and never had anot her mishap up to the fall of Sebastopol, 111 except the loss of two toes and the flesh off the bottoms of my feet, momentos of trench duty and had hoots. Arriving home,a lot of us went to Buck- ingham Palace,where our Queen pinned the distinguished medals on our breasts, and so ended my first campaign. I volunteered for the Main y in 's7,but the doctor said I no. However. I did manage to get to China in '6O, and helped to use the Armstrong guns for the first time in active service. This was the end of my war experience I was discharged December 5, 1874,having enlisted April 19, 1842. lam now in my sixty-ninth year, but if my services were required by my country, I would willingly go to the front to-day. My friends tell me I am "as nimble as a good many at forty, and only require to smell angry powder to bring all the old fire to life again." The following are the medals won by Mr. Hardy dur- ing his exciting and adventurous career :-1. Crimean medal and clasps for " Alma," " Balaclava," " Inker- man," " Sebastopol," 2, Turkish war medal. 3. Medal "for distinguished conduct in the field." 4 Sardinian war medal of" Merit." 5. China War medal, 1880, and clasps for" Taku Forts "and " Pekin." 6. Long ser- vice and good conduct medal.

Mr. Hardy fully deserves the honours he has received and we hope that no necessity for his being again "called out" may arise, but that on the contrary the remaining years of his life may be spent in peaceful happiness.

RUGBY.
WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.

Warrington played the first of their return matches on Thursday, when they met Leigh on the Wilderspool enclosure before 3,000 spectators. It will be remem- bered that it was Leigh which the Warrington team as at present constituted, first met in September. On that occasion, Leigh won by a pretty fair margin, although those who watched the game were firmly of opinion that when the teams met Warrington, the result would be reversed. The weather on Thursday was bitterly cold and the spectators and players experienced great discomfort, the latter especially, as the ground was hard with the frost. Mr. Underwood of Wigan was the referee, and the following was the Warrington team : Heesom, full back ; Barber, Burton, Cross' and Carey, three quarters ; Clark and Houghton, half backs ; Burrows, Nevins, Barrett, Wilcock, Hill, Andrews,Swift, and Taylor, forwards. Warrington won the toss, and took advantage of a stiff breeze which blew from goal to goal. Leigh kicked off,and were at once penned in their lines, and it looked odd son Warrington scoring but the visiting threequarters at length got the ball away,a ad chiefly by means of Spill- ane they reached the home quarter flag. Barber relieved, and Carey by a run and kick reached the half way line. Burrows upset Coop with the ball in his possession, and again Leigh had an anxious time. Carey made his mark, and kicking across to Burton, the latter dropped a mag- nificent goal from the touch line about five minutes from the start. Restarting, Heesom quickly sent Leigh to the right about, and although minus Taylor who had to retire hurt for a time, Warrington still pressed and a smart kick and follow up by Barrett almost resulted in a score. Cross was immediately afterwards prominent by a smart dribble which deserved a better fate. Heesom at length broke away with the ball and had almost a clear course to the line, when ene of the Leigh men deli- berately put out his foot and tripped him.severely hurt- ing him. This aroused strong feeling among the home spectators,who demanded that the player be sent off the field. The game was again restarted,and a fine outburst of passing between Clark, Burton,Cross, and Carey was spoiled by the latter mulling the ball,and the advantage was lost. A mark in a favourable position made by Tay- lor was disallowed, and Leigh at length reached half way. Heesom's kick was charged down, and three Leigh forwards had a clear course to the tine. Barber rushed after them at a great pace,and just as the Leigh players got the ball over the line,he kicked dead. Leigh attacked strongly after this, but Barber at length relieved the pressure, and the remaining portion of the half was in favour of Warrington,who led at half time by a dropped goal to nil. Hill's kick off after the interval was charged down, but the Warrington defence proved equal to the task ot repelling the danger. Clark was in particular playing a fine game at half. A dribble initiated by Houghton and supplemented by Nevins and Barber got the ball over the line but the final kick was too strong and the ball went dead. Clark again obliged with a strong run, and Wilcock got over but the point was disallowed, and a scrimmage ordered instead. A brief visit was paid to the Warrington line, but with no result for Warring- ton were soon attacking again. And Burton was particularly prominent by a run through the opposing team, and he was only stopped just in time. Foc a time Leigh pressed again chiefly being good play by Taylor and Walwork, but nothing but minors fell to their credit. Coop made a good bid for goal from a mark but only a minor resulted. At length a grand dribble took play to the opposite end, and Leigh had some narrow squeaks, Burrows on one occasion just fail- ing to ground the ball as it went over the dead ball line. When the final whistle was blown, Warrington were on the aggressive, bet nothing had lir.'en added during the last half, and a fast game had been won by. Warrington by a dropped goal (4 points) to nil.

RUNCORN v. 13 UNSI.EI'. The one attraction in Runcorn on Boxing Day was the football match on the Irwell-lane enclosure, when the Runcorn " Redtails " had as their opponents the' Hunslet team. A glance at the combination table showed the homesters to be in a far better position than their visi- tors, and ere the match began it was thought that the Cheshire lads would be more than equal for the burly Yorkshire men, especially when it was considered that the Hunslet team had the disadvantage of having played the previous day against the premier team of the corn- bination—Manningham, coupled with the further dis- advantage of the long railway journey from Yorkshire. The frost had nipped the Runcorn ground, and although it was in a hardened state it was thought fit to play upon. A piercing bleak wind swept across the ground and there was a dull grey heavy sky overhead. It was about three o'clock when the two teams stepped into the arena and there would be about 5,000 spectators present. The visiting team looked by far the more robus:, of the two, but as afterwards proved, what the homes ters lacked in bulk was more thancompensated for in agility. Faulkner—a name long associated with Runcorn football —commenced the game. There was nothing unusually exciting in the opening stages, but if anything the Run- corn men had the advantage of the play. A flutter of excitement was caused when Robinson made a noteworthy run through the thick of his opponents, later rt hspoiled n got ct epr ot ne tryio n n andrig a registeredssed against Hunslet, by passing the ball forward. A few mom t beau- tifully to Warder who was palled up near the line. Stoddart and Butterworth put in some good work for the homesters, and the threequarter lino worked well to- gether,but somehow or other when the finishing toueh was needed, it was missing. Cromer brought relief to the visitors by a smart run half the length of the field. Gilthorpe got possession, and passing in the nick of time to Hannah that player romped over the line triumphantly amid the applause of the few Yorkshiremen present. The kick at goal by Goldthorpe was a failure. This success seemed to put new life into the visiting team,who played with commendable dash. They compelled the homesters to touch down,and continued the pressure for some con- siderable time, but the defence of the Runcorn men was very safe. A. Goldthorpe gave Hannah another oppor- tunity to race over the line but he was knocked into touch when within an ace of scoring. Warder at length brought welcome relief to his side and the majority of the spectators by a clever run but a try was lost by erra- tic passing. Success, however, smiled upon Runcorn shortly afterwards, for the visitors' full back failing to catch the ball when near to his defensive line, enabled Lightfoot to score near the posts. The score was not further improved upon by the inevi- table geod kick. The whistle for half-time sounded almost immediately afterwards, the score sheet show- ing a try each. Some fine passing movements were witnessed after the restart, and it was not long before the locals were on the aggressive. The ball was carried over the visitors' lines, but the referee ruled it back. The homesters continued to press and W. Faulkner raced strongly over the line, scoring a fine try. Warder took the place kick but failed to improve the score. From this point to the end of the game there was no mistaking the best team. The visitors seemed to have blown off all their steam at once, and slowed down considerably. Their play fell away completely*, and perhaps it is not to be wondered at considering the claims which had been made upon their physical powers during the preceding 24 hours. It was seldom they again entered the homes- ters domain, and when they did so, it was for a very brief period. The Runcorn men seemed quite fresh in comparison with their opponents and were successful in registering a further ten points against them. Walker was responsible for one try which was further improved upen by Myers ; and J. Faulkner from a pass received from his brother VVilliam,scored the last try of the match which was again improved upon. An unpleasant incident during this half was the hooting of the referee by the spectators, on one occasion when he ruled against their opinion. A well contested game was finished in the twilight with the result : Runcorn 2 goals 2 tries (16 points), Hunslet 1 try (3 points. Hunslet have thus suffered their third defeat within six days, and the one administered by Runcorn is the severest of all. If the form displayed by Runcorn is maintained they have yet a chance of reaching the top rung of the ladder in the Northern Union. RUNCORN v. div.p: ITALTON.

Bocrucit. COMMITTEE.—A meeting of the Halton Parochial Committee was held in the Girl's School on Saturday afternoon. The Rev. G. D. Wray occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. T. Wright, Looker, Jeacock, Birch, Hughes, Ackerley, Bar- row, McCulloch, and J. Ashton iclerk). The resolution which had been passed by the District Council with regard to Halton Brook, were approved. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Looker, seconded by Mr. Hughes, that steps be taken for providing a supply of water for domestic pur- poses to the schools and to the seven houses on the com- mon.—The Clerk reported that Dr. Adams and Dr. Vacher, the county medical officer, were attending to Halton Brook that afternoon for the purpose of inspect- ing the same and the flow oisewage therein, and report- ing thereon in accordance with the resolution 6 f the last meeting of the committee, and Messrs. Jeacmck and McCulloch and Hughes were deputed to attend with the clerk to meet the medical gentlerm.u.—The report was approved at the meeting of the Rural Council, on the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr. Stokes. ST. TSCOMAS' CHARITY.On Saturday (St. Thomas' Day) there was distributed at the Girls' school, Halton, to windows and other deserving poor to the number of 49 in sums of 53. and 103., the sum of £22 153. being St. Thomas' Charity which is now a parochial one, and will be distributed annually by the Parish council. The fol- lowing were present at the distribution :—Ra G. D. Wray (vicar), Messrs. S. Barrow, J. Looker, C. Birch, J. Ackerley, H. Rowe, T. Wright, and A. Woodier (clerk). rillenry Wright, a labourer, was executed at Notting- ham on Tuesday for the murder of Mary Elizabeth Rey- nolds, a widow who had refused to marry him, and her two sons and grandson. Wright,after cutting the throats of his four victims, set fire to the house and then gave himself up to the police. •-_' ' • •

div.head: Eetttro to the Obitor.
div.p: Eetttro to the Obitor.

"COUNCILLOR A. BENNETT ON TIIE UNER- PLOYED AND IRELAND." Sir,—Mr. T. C. Dalton never appears to be happy un- less he is figuring in the correspondence columns of some local paper. Doubtless this is ore way to become famous, and I am sorry that I have not either the time or the in- clination to emulate him in the pleasing pursuit. And "the electors af Howley Ward," to whose attention he is good enough to recommend me, are quite capable of exercising the franchise without any assistance from him. But perhaps I may be permitted to observe that, if Mr. Dalton had been a member of the Warrington Debating Society as long as some of Us. he would know that it is usual to fight one's battles out upon the spot, and to say what one has got to say where it can be promptly an swered, and not toga home and invoke the assistance of the inkpot. As a matter of fact, Mr. Dalton's misrepresentation as to what I said in reference to the unemployed in opening the recent debate on " Imperial Federation," was ans- wered the same evening, and it is a little disingenuous of him to endeavour to reap a petty party advantage by repeating it. By wresting one's words from their con- tsst, reporting them for one's self, and ignoring your op- ponont's explanations, it is possible to prove anything ; but, if ever I was vain enough to think that I had made my meaning sufficiently clear, it was when I tried to show that one of the principal reasons why I advocated Imperial Federation was because of my sym- pathy with the unemployed, and because I believed that it would find them employment, first,by 'reviving British trade, and, secondly, by opening out new fields of enterprise in our noble colonies beyond the sea. My contention was that, if we had Free Trade throughout the Empire, which, I contend, would be the ultimate outcome of the policy which I propose, we should secure new markets for our manufactures,and increasing opportunities of occupation for our people ; and that, in addition to this, if England became too crowded, they might find- new homes, and even ampler opportunities, in that wider England which covers one- fifth of the surface of the globe. Surely it is better to grow rich on a Canadian homestead than to starve in a Warrington slum ! And it is Mr. Dalton who does not appear to have any remedy but the workhouse. Proba- bly my sympathy with suffering is just as keen as his, and it is not confined to Ireland. As to his lamentations over the woes of the middle ages—" let him weep !" Possibly the great Liberal who lopped a King's head off was responsible for a sufficient number of barbarities ; but there are too many contem- porary wrongs which need redressing to render it advis- able to waste much time in tearing one's hair over the cruelties of Oliver Cromwell.—Faithfully yours. ARTHUR BENNE TT. Warrington, 19th December, 1395.

THE PROPOSED NEW UNION INFIRHARY. Sir,—The meeting of the Warrington Board of Guar- dians held on the 11th inst., appears, from the report, to have been one of great importance and one which much interest seems to have been attached. The Rev, J. H. Riddette was, I think, fully justified in taking the course he did seeing that no or little reference was made. on the minutes as to the surprise visit which was paid to the Parlgate Schools by Mr. Jenner rust and two other officials of the Local Government Board. I was much interested in reading the debate aa to the proposed site of the new infirmary. Mr. Rickman op- posed the suggestion of purchasing the land adjoining the present buildings for several reasons. I should, how- ever, like to ask what would be the extra cost of build- ing if land was purchased at a lower rate, out in the country, as he suggests: Would not the material have to be carted out and the workmen allowed " travelling time," thereby increasing the cost considerably? Further what would the Guardians thidk of having to tramp out to every meeti-g, there ? They, would, I think, object ; and the old question of goinsrto a large expense in pro- viding suitable offices in town would thus be raised. If the latter were done how many times would the G ,ar- dians visit the Infirmary ? • I imagine it would be like the recent important meeting at Padgate were only five members were present out of a committee consisting of two-thirds of the whole of the Board. Something ought, most certainlr, to be done, and very speedily, to remedy the coadition of the present Infirmary buildings. I can speak from my own per- sonal observations that I was never in a more musty and miser able block of Infirmary buildings. The very at- mosphere of the place is sufficient to hasten the end of every patient whose unhappy lot it is to "enter there." The buildings, as was stated, are bordered on one side by a smallpox hospital, on another by a railway, and on a third by a ditch, and are also overshadowed by the lofty water tower of the workhouse itself. In this con- fined area and under these unfavourable circumstances how is it possible for the patients to breathe freely? Mention was also made as to the approach to the Infirmary and it was stated that "There was quite an avenue of privies to pass through before the gates of the house could be reached." This is certainly the case,but, if the land adjoining the premises were purchased would it not be possible to have an entrance to the Infirmary from Lovely Lane. I was speaking some time ago to a person on the same subject when ha very abruptly informed me that "it did not really matter in the least, for the sooner the patients died the better; they're only paupers." This, of course, is one way of looking at it; but, is it the way in which we, as Christ,ans, should treat our aged and istirm poor? Apologizing for having taken open much of your valuable space, which I should not have done had not the matter been of so urgent a necessity.—Yours truly,
VIVIAN GREY.

Sir,—Mr. R. T. Fairclough's last letter is about the silliest effusion which has been offered to the notice of your readers for many a day. The most sensiblekremark it contains is the writer's assertion that the letter in question is his " last reply " on the subjects in dispute. If Mr. Faircloneh had been wise he would have left public correspondence alone, as whatever abilities lie may have in other directions, letter writing is certainly not his " forte." So far as the question of Messrs. Bishop's wharf is con- cerned. I have on several public occasions in the Council Chamber stated why, in the interests of our trade, the increasing of our rateable property, aiad as a means of providing employment for some few men at least who at present have nothing to do, it icon every possible public ground desirable that the necessary permission should he g• ranted I am convinced too that the bulk of the opposition to the proposals was and is prompted by per- sonal and selfish motives, and it is quite clear thst the latter opinion predominated in Fairfield ward at the last election as Mr. Faircl.'ugh has realised by the defeat whith he then sustained. I should, therefore, not have noticed Mr. Fairclough's first letter at all if it had not been for the tmgentle- manly manner in which he went out of his way to throw mud at the firm with which lam associated I was then compelled to intervene, with the result that, as I shewn by Mr. Fairclough's own admission in his last letter, I have proved him to be in the wrong all along the line. The insinuation contained in his first letter was that the WS rring.ton Slate Co. had improperly acquired a wharf which had formerly belonged to the public. In my reply I showed that my firm have paid rent to the owners of the wharf from the very first day of our tenancy, so that our conduct is quite free from reproach in the matter. When a "gentleman." publicly makes a mis-statement reflecting upon the actions of others,it is customary for an apology to be tendered. Is it to much to exp•ct an apology from Mr. R. T. Fairclough ? Again. Mr. Fairclough admits that his father used the wharf above ref3rrecl tn for years without payment, for many years down to IE6I, the time that he vacated the adjoining premises. That is exactly my point as stated n my last letter, viz., that " the discharging of grain free of toll occurred at the time when Mr. Fairclough's father rented the old Pottery from Messrs. Joseph Cros- field and Sons," and when the tenancy of the "adjacent premises " ceased, the right to discharge grain, or any- thing else free of toll, ceased also. If my version of the facts is not correct, why did not Messrs. Fairclough coo- tinue to discharge their grain at the same place " free of toll ? "1 think I may venture to say without offence that if" freedom from toll "of any kind is obtains hie. my friends, Messrs. Fairclough are not usually the last to be in at it. Now as to the public road past Litton's Mill, I main- tain absolutely the statements made in my last letter. The read was and is in my opinion, a public cartway, and its present obstruction is unjustifiable. I can almost "hear" the incredulous smile which would creep over the faces of your readers when they perused Mr. R. T. Fairclough's statement "that to avoid litigation, we adopted other plans," &c. .a Finally, as to Mr. Fairclough's retention of his position on the Upper Mersey Commission, of course there is such a thing as "good taste," deference to public opinion,and regard for precedents. Perhaps it is too much to expect Mr. R. T. Fairclough to be im- pressed by minor considerations of this sort, but if he desires to serve the best interests of the town, he will at once retire from a position which was conferred upon him by a majority of the Town Council, on the distinct understanding that such appointment should only he held by a member of the Town Council. It is not very long since Mr. R. T. Fairclough prevented the re-election of the late Alderman Davies and got himself installed- in the position on precisely these grounds. Why is Mr. Fairclough so anxious to retain his untemunerative position ? Is it his over excessive desire for the public welfare or is it an illustration of the Lancashire man's advice to his son, "If ever theau does owt for nowt, do it for thrsel " ; I leave your readers to judge for them- selves.—Faithfully yours,
U. ROBERTS.

NEWTON-LE-WILOWS C EIO q.A.L A. ND MUSICAL SOCIETY.
FIRST ANNUAL CONCERT.

On Saturday evening a fairly large and fashionable audience assembled at the Town Hall, Newton, to enjoy the first concert promoted by the above society. For several years Newton were in possession of a choral society, of which, Mr. Peter Fairclough was the con- ductor and this was in the habit of annually presenting to large audiences some excellent cantatas and mis- cellaneous selections of solos; but for some reason or other in the later years of its existence, the programmes were not executed with the excellence which character- ised the early productions. For two years,there has been a blank, but certain of the music-loving people of New- ton did not view the absence of a musical society from their midst with favour, and eonsequently some few months ago invitations were issued to past members of choral societies and others, to join in an endeavour to form a choral or orchestral society. The effort met with unqualified success and a strong society was got together, and after engaging Mr. F. EL Crossley of War- rington as 'conductor, operations were at once com- menced. It was decided to take in hand the cantata " Joan of Arc," for early production, and this was the piece which was submitted for the delectation of the audience on Saturday night. To the cre lit of the con- ductor, and the choir, it must be said, that their several practices have got been without effect, for this difficult cantata,bristling with intricate passages was produced in a manner which called forth the hearty applause of the audience. Of course the principal parts were allotted to artistes not directly connected to the society, but ; apart from this thr choruses were rendered in a most efficient and pleasing manner. .The principals engaged to assist were :—S4prano, Miss F. Hiller, Manchester concerts, who took the part of " Joan of Arc." Tenor, Mr. Ben Roberts, Liverpool Pro-Cathedral, " Phillips, a youth of Humid:lly." Baritone, Mr. W. H. Wallington, Warrington, Robert de Baudricourt, Provost of Van- coleurs, and Jean de Noveloupont, or gentleman of Metz. Mr. A. E. VVykes, presided at the piano,. and Ar. P. Fairclough, organ. Assistance was also rendered the band by Mr. R. Pearson, first violin ; Mr. J. H. Peplow, second violin, Mr. J. Shaw, viola ; Mr.Crossley, 'cello, Mr. R. Whitfield, double base. The principals all acquitted themselves exccedMgly well, Miss Hiller, gain- ing warm apprec,ation for the song "A sing, a simple ring." Tills lady and Mr. Roberts created a pleasing imnresqion by their excellent rendering of the tuneful " Full fl)ws the river." Mr. Wallington secured the hearty plaudits of the audience for the patriotic song " Who would not fight for freedom." As we have said the choruses were well sustained, excellent time being kept, showing that Mr: Crossley as conductor had the choir well in hand.

The second part of the programme consisted of mis- cellaneous items, and opened with an intermezzo " For- get me not "by the band, Mr. Ben Roberts following with the song" Come into the Garden,Maud," for the ex- cellent rendering of which he gaine I an encore, and gave " The anchor's weighed." Miss Florence Hiller received a vociferous encore for the song " For all eternity," the violin obligato being well played by Mr. F. H. Crossley. In response to the recall she sang with much pathos "The Lost Chord." A violin solo " Bolero" by Mr. F.H. Crossley was redernanded, but he simoly acknowledged the compliment. The choir sang "Oh ! sing to God " with much emphasis, Miss Hiller giving the solo. Mr. W. H. Wallington for" I would I were a King " was recalled, and the choir terminated the programme with the chorus "The gallant Troubadour" with orchestral accompaniment.

div.head: JAMES SKELLANG.
div.p: JAMES SKELLANG.
A REPLY TO MR. PEERS.

Sir,-11r. John Peers is a unique personality, and is in his peculiar fashion irresistible and unapproachable. What an embodiment of wisdom and learning he is ! Like the daring rider on his barebacked steed of some circus he vaults and jumps over obstacles until his per- formances are watched with wonder, or with the clown in the ring he bubbles forth his witticisms and causes the yokels to grin immensely. But we like him best standing on his own hillock, and crowing cock-a- doodle-doo,and in shrillest tones, piping his treble notes, and with feathers ruffled, and cock-a-doodle-doo swagger, until all inferior creatures have no place in creation.

Yet he is an obscurantist scribbler, a Dioge.nes in his tub, with his negative babblement and palaverings ! His reproach of I:l.is men is not very dignified. " Mr. Missionary "is not worth so much as a sneer ! John Peers has no statu quo in the Christian Church by reason of his own admission! Confucius or Christ ? John Peers which ? Be honest and say if you dare that Jesus Christ is inferior to any other mortal teacher ? We believe Him superior to all other. I appeal to you and other secularists for Christ's gospel and its grand princi- ples. Keen satire, misty surmises, slang terms, are " highly low !" Voltaire, flu me,Paine, and others were competent detractors and understood the science of abuse. The modern men " are deists in theory—Pagans in inclihation,and Atheists in practice." o er the water, or " Beyond the realms of chaos and old night." " Let the missionary tub" (John Peers is not elegant) " stand on its own bottom—if it has one " that is the sting! What about Moses, or Jesus or Paul ? What about Genesis, or Isaiah, or Christianity— if it has none ! Now this is the " sweet reasonableness of Mr. John Peers, the apostle of negations, the local preacher of evolution, its querulousness, and stark pes- simism. My good friend don't attempt to:, much. Ba. warned by the past, and dispassionately consider. Mis- sionaries ? Luther, Cromwell,George Fox.Wesley,Co.rey, Living,stoue, and many another grand soldier of Christ has done noble work for the world. Never mind your cheap, sneer about " the utility of carrying religious frying pan 3 and blankets to Timbucto -)." Here is mat- ter for thought in another letter, which a newspaper brings t ) me from Queensland,in which I read," Slavery in Africa still means the expenditure of more than a thougand lives weekly. On tue east coast of Africa 64,000 lives are sacrificed yearly, and for the Zanzibar slave trade 24,000 yearly." The precepts of the New Testament are teaching men to abolish slavery, and freedom and liberty will be in the future, the birthright of all mankind, and Christ's kingdom reign and his sub- jects will be happy and prosperous.—Yours _truly.. Dec. 18, 1806.

A couple of dialogues were also given, ” April Fools " and Dr. Diaculum," the characters being sustained in an able manner. Lea and male voices; chorus " Behall the Lamb," choir; air "He was despised," Miss A. Moly- neux; chorus " Hallelujah" choir. THE DROWNING OF A GOLBORNE MIN.

An inquest was held at the Wargrave Inn, New- ton, on Saturday, by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, on the body of William Smith. collier, of Golbsrne, who was found drowned in the Sankey Canal under circumstances detailed in our last issue.—Betsy Smith, ot 40, Church-st.,Golborne,said deceased was her husband, and was 49 years of , age. He left home at ten minutes past six to go to see a friend of his named George Hill, game keeper. at Burtonwood, and she never saw him alive again.—George Hill said demised was a dis- tant relative of his. He visited him on Saturday. and he arrived at nine o'clock and left again about six o'clock at night. Witness accompanied him part of the road,and they parted at the" Fiddle in Bag" heerhouse. They had two glasses of beer there,and deceased had the to walk along the canal bank. Witness never Raw him alive again.—P.C. William- son deposed to finding the body on Thursday about 12.30. There wa4 no mark of violence, but one leg was broken, presumably by a passing boat. A ver- dict, of" Found drowned " was re-urned. CHRISTMAS DAY AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. Tht, Sf.n.SO'l of festive gatherings was observed in a remarkably quiet manner at Earlostown and Newton: It has been the custom in previous years for several choirs of carol singers, chiefly from the various places of worship, to turn out on Christmas Eve, in order to herald with song the advent of Christmas day. 'the custom, however, appears to hare fallen into disuse, and this year carol singers were conspicuous by their absence. Probably this was due to tile ex.cessive cold weather which pre- vailed, a keen high wind blowing from the South East, which rendered pedestrianism a discomfort. The Viaduct works brass and, however, hravei the elements, and from an early hour until midnight discoursed sacred music appropriate to the season, in different parts of the district. They turned out again on Christmas morning, and completed the round about noon. There was no improvement in the weather. rind there were very few people astir. At the various churches service was held, but they were only very poorly attended. In the afternoon the Earlestown football team jou-neyed to Hindley . to play off their return Alliance fixture with that club, and returned victorious by 4 goals to 1.

div.head: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: NEWTON URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday afternoon in the Board room at Dutton Work- house. Mr. J. Mclntyre, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present :—Admiral Parry,Messrs. Joseph Knowles, J. Weir, T. Lewis, J. Stokes, T. Wright, C. Mounfield, C. W. Davenport, C. Roylance, J. Spruce,W. Holt, W. Bradford, J. Datbyshire, S. Woodward, H. E. Heywood, J. Spruce, J. Brandreth, J. Whitlow,G.Priest- ner, and Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), Messrs. Swinton and Diggle (surveyors), and Mr. J. Farrington (nuisance inspector).
SUTTON WATER SUPPLY.

Writing on behalf of the Parish Council of Sutton,Mr. James Robinson stated that it was resolved " That a report of the scheme to supply the township with water be sent to the Sanitary Authority of the Runcorn District Council." He enclosed a report of the scheme, setting forth that a connection be made with the Vyrrawy water mains of the Liverpool Corporation (who had agreed to supply the township with water at the rate of 91. per 1,000 gals.) at the top of Sutton, where the road to Preston Brook is crossed by the water mains. He then gave a description of the line of pipes and their size after which it is stated that the laying of the pipes would supply all the district, except the cottages near Frodsham Bridge and Frodsham Bridge mill, which it was proposed to supply by an arrangement with the Frodsham Parish Council. It was estimated that the scheme would coat £7OO, of which amount the trustees of the Aston estate (as owners of the chief part of pro- perty in the township) would pay £4OO. It was pro- posed to borrow the £3OO from the Local Government Board for 30 years, to be repaid as might be directed. —The Chairman said the scheme was a good one, and would be likely to meet the difficulty.—Mr. Stokes asked if alas well upon which so much money had been spent was a failure.—The Inspector: Yes, it is.—Mr. Wood- ward moved that the Clerk intimate to the Parish Coun- cil that a detailed estimate, &c., would be repaired btfore the scheme could be submitted to the Local ' Government Board, and that the Clerk have an inter- view with Mr. Thomas Rigby, chairman of the Parish Council, with reference to the subject.—This was agreed to.

div.head: ALLEGED BONE TRUCK NUISANCE AT FRODSHAIE.
div.p: THE ALLEGED BONE TRUCK NUISANCE AT FRODSHAIE.

Mr. Cherles Linaker again wrote stating that the bone nuisance at Frodsham still continued. On Monday last, he added, there were seven or eight trucks, and in the middle of the day the smell was abominable. Instead of abating it, it was still on the increase.—Mr. Heywood moved, and Mr. Woodward seconded that a copy of the letter be sent to the Railway Company.—This was agreed to.

div.head: PATH ACROSS THE LOCKS AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: THE PATH ACROSS THE LOCKS AT LATCHFORD.

A communication was read from Mr. Marshall Stevens , nfanager of the Ship Canal Company,stating that he had made enquiries with reference to the approaching and lighting arrangements at Latchford Locks,from which it appeared that the facilities of access to the footway and general lighting arrangements were quite satisfactory. If the Council had any suggestions to put forward they would be pleasedto consider them,but he might mention that the Ship Canal Company was under no obligation to provide lights• across the locks. The diffi- culty they had to contend with was that the public instead of proceeding direct across the locks, often wandered about on the island, andi par- ticularly so when vessels happened to be passing through the locks.—The Clerk said he had forwarded a copy of the letter to the Grappenhall Parish Council. Ile could not find anything in the Ship Canal Acts that compelled them to light the foot path.—Mr. Bradford stated that there had been a footpath at that point from time immemorial.—Mr. Wood ward considered that that being the case tbe company were obliged to take steps to'make the footpath safe for passengers.—Mr. Bradford stated that a man had fallen into the lock at the point in question, and been drowned since the last meeting of the Council.—The subject was deferred until it had been further discussed by the Grappenhall Parish Council.
THE HEALTH AND -SANITARY CONDITION OF EINGSLEY

Dr. Adams reported with reference.to the health of Kingsley. He said it was one of the healthiest townships in the district during the past twelvemonths, and that the principal insanitary spat was the Kingsley Home for Boys, the requirements for which were insuffi- cient, and on which he had reported some time ago. In answer to a question by Mr. Woodward, respecting the sanitary condition of Kingsley,the Inspector reported that the township was quite equal to any of the scattered townships situated within the district. He granted that there were one or two minor improvements which might be made, and these were not being lost sight of, and wonld be brought under the notice of the Council in due course if required.—The reports were considered gener- ally satisfactory. THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

Mr. Farrington submitted a certificate of analysis of water from pump and well at cottages in Runcorn road, Moore, which was not satisfactory. It was decided to forward a copy of Um certificate to tha owner.—An application was read by the Inspector from Mr. 0. E. Linaker fsir certificate of occupation for four houses near Sutton dock belonging to Mr. I'. Speakman, of Runcorn. The contemplated water supply was not coneidered altogether satisfactory.—A complaint was read from the Clerk to tho Dare bury School Board, respecting untrapped road inlets near to the school.—The Inspector reported that posters relating to infectious diseases had I been forwarded to all the schools in the district with the etception of Halton and Grappeuhall which were closed. This concluded the business.

THE ANGLO-AIIEitICA.N CRISIS.
THE DEFENCES OF CANADA: INtERVIEW WITH A CANADIAN GENERAL.

A representative of Reuter' s Agency on Saturday had an interview with General J. Millburn Laurie. M.P. hr Pembroke, who served for over twenty years in all parts of Canada, Nova Scotia, and British Columbia. and re- presented a Canadian constituency in the Dominion Parliament, and who only arrived from Canada a few days ago. Dealing first with President Cleveland's at- titude, he said : While firmly believing it to be an ele, • tioneering kite, it must be recognised that there is a large amount of very inflammable material in the United States, to which the President has applied the match and which may at any moment ignite and get beyond con- trol. There is, therefore, very serious risk of certain hot-heads on the American side, near the frontier, at- tacking what they hate more than anything else—the British flip. So far as Canada is concerned, the chief danger lies in some small party of Jingoes in n moment of excitement crossing the frontier and insulting our flag in a way that would at once call for reprisals. You will thus see the danger of cool-headed people being embroiled by a few hot-headed, irresponsible Indivi- duals. As for Canada's position, there is a very strong national feeling in the Dominion. The Canada militia is largely composed of young men who pass out of the ranks as soon as they settle clown in their ordinary avocations, but should emergency arise they would in- stantly place their services at the disposal of the Govern- ment. I may quote one instance of what they have done. At the time of the Fenian raid, when General M‘Deugall ordered a corps whose full effective strength was 10,000 to assemble at certain points within torty- eilit the members were scattered over the country following their civil occupations, over 14,000 men assembled within the specified time. Again, during the North-west rebellion, when the Queen's Own from Toronto was ordered at reduced strength to Winnipeg, those left out were so anxious to serve that they actually paid their own fares to Winnipeg in order that they might boon the spot to fill the vacan- cies caused by casualties. Others holding commissions served as privates rather than be left out. That wOula occur again,only to a greater extent than before. The actual force of Canada is only a skeleton force. Corn- panies have been reduced to 39 men,but in case of war they would be immediately raised to 100 man, vacancies being rapidly filled by retired members still in their youth. In the event of war Canada could immediately place 100,000 trained men in the field, not unwilling servants, but every one filled with the highest loyalty to the mother country and fired with the utmost enthu- siasm. Regarding the vulneratoility of the frontier, General Laurie said : Although Canada has only five million people, they are, for the most part, within strik- ing distance of the frontier, whilst the population of the United States, although their frontier is more thickly populated, are to a large extent a great distance off. It is not, therefore, a question of 66 millions versus five millions. It would take a much longer time for the United States to bring up some of their forces than it would to send troops from England. There•is no ques- tion that the Canadians are united in their determina- tion to defend their country and to remain part of the British Empire. As compared with the United States C made, is str.nger to-day than she was in 1812, and at the end of 1812-4 war not enly was there not a single American soldier on Canadian ;mil, but, on the contrary, Canada had taken possession of the peninsular of Michi- gan which, but for the action of the home authorities she would still possess. The feeling in Canada is per- fectly friendly towards the United States provided she minds her own business, but once she commences to In- terfere with Cana iian affairs there is not a man in the Dominion who will not cry " Hands off!" The French Canadians, too, are just as solid against the idea of be- ing absorbed into the United States, and I have the ; highest opinion of them. They are just as ready to re- ski American invasion as they were when 400 French Canadians drove back 1.800 Amerinan s sldiers. A MESSAGE FROM MR. GLADSTONE. Nisv YORK, SATIIRDAY,—The "New York World" announces that it has received the following cablegram from Mr. Gladstone, in reply t 4 a request for a statement by hiin on the present situation :7•-" Hawarden.—l dare not interfere. Only common sense is recmirel. I cannot say more with ad vantn.ge.—GLADTONN]." The request cabled tc England by the jaurnal was worded as follows: —" American sentiment is at a turning paint. Once turned the wrong way, no power on earth can hold it lack. In the American mind you, mora than any score of other men, and more than the Government, epitomise the British people. A word of peace and fellowship from you will aid to check clamour, soothe passion, encourage sober thought, and may avert a calamity."

The following telegram has been received by the editor of the " Now York World " :—" Sandringham. December 211. " Sir Frances Knollys is desired by the Prince of Wales and the Duks of York to thank Mr. Pulitzer for his cablegram. They earnestly trust and cannot but believe that the present crisi; will be arranged in a manner satisfactory to both countries, and will be succeeded by the same warm feeling of friendship which has existed between them for so many years."

The book is conveniently divided into 12 chapters. The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty,nr when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out the best age for marriage, and WllO should have children and who not, and furnishea useful in- formation that one can ordinarily get only from an in- tell,gent doctor. The third chapter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four treats of the signs of pregnancy. The fifth chapter tells how a woman should live eluring the pregnant state. The sixt'a cha,ter traits of mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats cf maternal impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due tolongings on the part of the mother, but rather to her pour health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic physician says that confinements can be made comparatively easy If certain rules are obeyed ; these; rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confinement until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat the mother till she is up mad about again. The eleventh chapter treats of sterility ; gives the main dauses of it, how these may be overcome and children result. The last chapter treats of the •' change," a most important article for all w•lmeri over forty. The book is full Of useful information and no book is written which goes so thotoughly into matters relating to married women.
